# Craft-cards provenance map

Out-of-runtime maintainer record. Neither consumer receives this file: a card carries the rule, its numbers and a compact `## Source` locator; this map carries the full citation with its fetch status, the topic and research note the card came from, the formulation source where a practitioner text supplied the wording, the reception, and the maintenance notes. Round-trip rule: a card plus its line here plus its topic's research note reconstruct everything known about the rule.

One line per card: `rule_id · evidence citation(s) with fetch status and the quoted statement · topic (research note) · formulation source · reception · notes` (evidence strength, ownership, caveats).

Fetch status per citation, as the design note's source policy defines it: `fetched` — opened from the authoring environment and quoted; **relayed** — the search index's statement of the claim, quoted, the paper itself unopened; **unfetched** — cited from memory, never a card's only anchor. A relayed or unfetched citation is openable by any reader and stands to be re-verified.

---
## CODE — code inside a function
- **CODE-01** · PMD, Java rule `LinguisticNaming`, category codestyle, since 6.7.0 (pmd/pmd, pmd-java/src/main/resources/category/java/codestyle.xml, rule description; defaults in pmd-java/src/main/java/net/sourceforge/pmd/lang/java/rule/codestyle/LinguisticNamingRule.java: booleanMethodPrefixes and booleanFieldPrefixes is, has, can, have, will, should; transformMethodNames to, as; checkTransformMethods false; checkFields and checkVariables true; ignoredAnnotations java.lang.Override; checkSetters skips a setter whose return type is the enclosing type; isBooleanType accepts an unboxed boolean, java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicBoolean and java.util.function.Predicate; the constructor registers only method, field and local-variable declarations, `super(ASTMethodDeclaration.class, ASTFieldDeclaration.class, ASTLocalVariableDeclaration.class)`, so formal parameters are never checked; commented out of rulesets/java/quickstart.xml), fetched: "This rule finds Linguistic Naming Antipatterns. It checks for fields, that are named, as if they should be boolean but have a different type. It also checks for methods, that according to their name, should return a boolean, but don't. Further, it checks, that getters return something and setters won't. Finally, it checks that methods, that start with "to" - so called transform methods - actually return something, since according to their name, they should convert or transform one object into another. There is additionally an option, to check for methods that contain "To" in their name - which are also transform methods. However, this is disabled by default, since this detection is prone to false positives." · SCANL Identifier Name Structure Catalogue (SCANL/identifier_name_structure_catalogue, README.md § Linguistic Antipatterns), fetched, reproducing the catalogue of Arnaoudova, Di Penta, Antoniol, 'Linguistic antipatterns: what they are and how developers perceive them', Empirical Software Engineering 21(1):104–158, 2016, DOI 10.1007/s10664-014-9350-8 (**relayed**): "Is returns more than a Boolean [...] the return type is not Boolean but rather a more complex type thus allowing a wider range of values without documenting them. [...] Set method returns [...] A set method having a return type different than void without proper documentation of the return type/values. [...] Expecting but not getting single instance [...] The name of a method indicates that a single object is returned but the return type is a collection. [...] Validation method does not confirm [...] the method neither provides a return value informing whether the validation was successful, nor documents how to proceed to understand. [...] Get method does not return [...] The name suggests that the method returns something (e.g., name starts with "get" or "return") but the return type is void. The documentation should explain where the resulting data is stored and how to obtain it. [...] Not answered question [...] The name of a method is in the form of predicate whereas the return type is not Boolean. [...] Transform method does not return [...] there is no return value and it is not clear from the documentation where the result is stored. [...] Expecting but not getting a collection [...] The name of a method suggests that a collection should be returned but a single object or nothing is returned. [...] Method name and return type are opposite [...] The intent of the method suggested by its name is in contradiction with what it returns. [...] Says one but contains many [...] It is unclear whether a change aspects one or multiple instances in the collection. [...] Name suggests boolean but type is not [...] The name of an attribute suggests that its value is true or false, but its declaring type is not Boolean. [...] Says many but contains one [...] The name of an attribute suggests multiple instances, but its type suggests a single one. [...] Attribute name and type are opposite [...] The use of antonyms can induce wrong assumptions." · Eclipse JFace `ControlEnableState.disable`, the catalogue's example of Method name and return type are opposite (eclipse-platform/eclipse.platform.ui, bundles/org.eclipse.jface/src/org/eclipse/jface/dialogs/ControlEnableState.java, master), fetched, documented in its source: "Saves the current enable/disable state of the given control and its descendents in the returned object; the controls are all disabled. [...] @return an object capturing the enable/disable state" · the same paper, abstract (Google Scholar snippet in a third-party crawl, AndresPonciano/finalprojectforsure data/elasticsearchScripts/data_finalfiles_ndjson/GIULIANOANTONIOL.json, **relayed**): "The aim of this work is to identify recurring poor practices related to inconsistencies among the naming, documentation, and implementation of an entity—called Linguistic Antipatterns (LAs)—that may impair program understanding. To this end, we first mine examples of such inconsistencies in real open-source projects and abstract them into a catalog of 17 recurring LAs related to methods and attributes." · the same paper, abstract, perception results (search-summary relay naming https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10664-014-9350-8, **relayed**): "Results showed that the majority of participants perceive LAs as poor practices and therefore must be avoided—69% and 51% of the external and internal developers, respectively." — the qualitative majority is also relayed by Peruma, Mkaouer, Decker, Newman, 'An empirical investigation of how and why developers rename identifiers', IWoR 2018, DOI 10.1145/3242163.3242169 (full-text copy in stefanik12/gensim_lda, **relayed**): "finding that the majority of programmers perceive anti-patterns as poor naming practices" · Fakhoury, Ma, Arnaoudova, Adesope, 'The Effect of Poor Source Code Lexicon and Readability on Developers' Cognitive Load', ICPC 2018, pp. 286–296, DOI 10.1145/3196321.3196347 (abstract from an IEEE Xplore metadata mirror, NicolasV15/CIRDC-Pro articleInfo/Conferences/1003168/8961319.json; DOI from BibSLEIGH, bibtex/bibtex.github.io ICPC-2018-FakhouryMAA.html; **relayed**): "we explore the effect of poor source code lexicon and readability on developers' cognitive load as measured by a cutting-edge and minimally invasive functional brain imaging technique called functional Near Infrared Spectroscopy (fNIRS). PoP1 §1.1 Names, 'Be accurate' (the inTable example); Clean Code ch. 2 'Avoid Disinformation' (accountList that is not a List); APOSD ch. 14 §14.3 'Names should be precise' (paraphrase, **unfetched**) · reception: not contested · notes: confidence moderate — the defect definitions are fetched and a static-analysis rule enforces the predicate, get, set and conversion cases, while the cost rests on two relayed abstracts (one developer survey, one fNIRS study); the perception search could not be re-run in the first drafting session (search budget exhausted), and the 69%/51% figures, from a search relay neither the drafter nor the skeptic could re-run verbatim, are not carried in the card; the card carries the qualitative majority from the Peruma et al. copy; in an earlier revision WebSearch answered twice with a summary restating the figures ("69% and 51% of the external and internal developers, respectively"; "69% of the external developers and 51% of the internal developers") without naming the result that carries the sentence, and a search restricted to link.springer.com did not state them, so the figures stay out; the catalogue's examples and the tool rule are Java; the card flags a subset of the catalogue: it accepts a documented mismatch in every case but the antonym rows, although Not answered question and the plurality rows carry no documentation clause; the antonym rows are excepted because the catalogue's own example, ControlEnableState.disable, is documented in its source (eclipse-platform/eclipse.platform.ui ControlEnableState.java, fetched; the comment is already present at tags R2_1 and R3_0); it reaches no parameter, since the catalogue covers methods and attributes and the static-analysis rule registers only method, field and local-variable declarations; it reads the plurality and antonym cases on fields, properties and routines only; number is read only in a noun phrase that names what a field or property holds or what a routine returns, alone or after get or return, since the catalogue's method rows condition on what the name says is returned; a noun phrase ending in a container word counts as plural, the reading the container-word pattern dispatches; a promise, future or task is read as the value it resolves to (TS1065 forces Promise<boolean> on an async predicate and Promise<T[]> on an async plural getter), and a set routine may return only a promise, error or result that carries nothing; dispatch gap: no pattern matches an antonym pair, a plural name on a single value or a collection type written without its element type (demonstrated by the skeptic with the corpus pre-pass on the catalogue's own examples), and a pattern for them would match no line of the Example, which is at its ten-line cap, so the Limits state the gap; the container-word pattern accepts PascalCase names so exported Go fields and C# properties dispatch; the behaviour-level and comment-level rows (Get more than accessor, Not implemented condition, Method signature and comment are opposite, Attribute signature and comment are opposite) are left to the routine-behaviour and comments topics; clippy wrong_self_convention was dropped because it checks how a conversion method takes its receiver, not its return type or plurality.

The Practice of Programming ch. 1 §1.1 Names, "Be accurate" (inTable returning true when the object is not in the table; paraphrase, **unfetched**) and "Use active names for functions"; Clean Code ch. 17 heuristic N7 "Names Should Describe Side-Effects" (getOos → createOrReturnOos, the source of the get-or-create wording); The Pragmatic Programmer 20th anniversary ed., Topic 44 "Naming Things", Tip 74 "Name Well; Rename When Needed" (the body changed under an unchanged name); johnousterhout/aposd-vs-clean-code README, "Method Length" (fetched: "If a reader trusts the name `isMultipleOfNthPrimeFactor` (which suggests a predicate with no side effects) and doesn't bother to read its code, they will not realize that it has side effects") · reception: not contested — in the same discussion the Clean Code author concedes the buried side effect ("Now that you've pointed it out I don't like it much"); no canon text defends a query-named routine that hides a write · notes: confidence moderate; the fetched evidence is normative official documentation from five languages (Swift and Python bind a name to its effect; Kotlin, Ruby and Julia name the mutating and copying forms of a pair apart, Ruby and Julia by marking the mutating form) plus one default-on lint whose reach is narrow (a getter returning a different field when a same-named field exists), and the research is relayed from abstracts and a catalogue, measuring cognitive load (fNIRS) and stating comprehension effort and wrong assumptions as the expected cost, not defect rates, so the severity rests on the lint's "most likely a bug" and the measured load; the predicate-truth clause rests on the relayed antipattern definition and the Boolean-assertion guideline, with no dedicated tool rule; the getter clause follows the lint's shape (another field returned where a same-named field exists), so a getter that returns a copy of, or a value computed from, its own field writes nothing and passes, and the catalogued getImageData example counts through its field write (this.imageData = new ImageData(...)); find, fetch and compute are left out of the query forms: no fetched or relayed text names them as words that promise no write; count is left to how it reads, as a noun accessor (which the lint reaches: clippy fires on fn count(&self) -> &u32 { &self.total } when a count field exists) or as a verb, and the cited guideline gives imperative verb phrases to routines with side effects; the documentation exemption reaches a get accessor only, following the fuller relayed row, while noun-phrase, predicate and conversion names are held to the name alone, since the Swift side-effect rule and the PEP 8 property note carry no documentation clause; the card does not carry the EMSE 2016 perception percentages (the relayed abstract is truncated before them), the "does more than it says / does the opposite" family names (not in any relayed text), the PoP inTable example (unfetched paraphrase), or Rust API guidelines C-CONV (fetched, but it states the cost and ownership of as_/to_/into_, not their side effects); the cache exemption follows PEP 8, while the log-line and interface-fixed-name bounds in Limits follow from the card's own definition of observable state, and so does the read bound, which passes a read that leaves its source unchanged and counts a consuming read from a held stream, queue or iterator as a write, as the fetched Julia style guide states for IO ('`read(io)` mutates `io`'); the self/this field-write and mutating-call triggers and the statement-level write trigger (a bare, @-prefixed or receiver-qualified name incremented or compound-assigned, or an @-prefixed or receiver-qualified field assigned) run on most object-oriented diffs by design, to reach a body changed under an unchanged name; a plain assignment to, or a mutating call on, an implicit-receiver field (count = 0; items.add(x);) is reached only when another added line of its hunk matches, since no pattern tells it from a local without matching every assignment; the query-word pattern also takes the bare word (get(, Get(, has(), and the accessor pattern takes property-accessor syntax (get {, get =>, get() =, Name =>, a computed var name: Type {)

Words over letters: the two letters-versus-words experiments above, the C# conventions, the Google Python guide, clang-tidy and clippy. Letters are fine: Beniamini et al. 2017, Go Code Review Comments ('Prefer c to lineCount'), the Google TypeScript guide (10-line tolerance), Linux kernel coding style, and the neverworkintheory review (2021-08-09), which calls the 19% difference "fairly small" and "not worth worrying about". The card resolves the dispute with two sourced conditions: whether the letter is conventional in its role, and whether a documented language or project convention allows short local names · notes: confidence moderate. Two experiments that compared letters with words found words better; the timed one found a modest 19% effect on finding semantic defects, none on finding syntax errors, in snippets in which every identifier used one style, and it counts speed, not defect rates. A third, Beniamini et al. 2017, gave single letters to local variables of limited scope or to substantial variables representing data structures (relayed: WebSearch summary of https://www.cs.huji.ac.il/w~feit/papers/SingleLetter17ICPC.pdf) and failed to show a significant difference in ability to modify the code; the card carries that result as the bound of the measured cost, not as support for conventional letters. Schankin et al. 2018 (DOI 10.1145/3196321.3196332) is not carried: its conditions were short single-word and long descriptive compound names (Table 1), so it compares words with phrases, which the Limits put outside the rule. Pylint's `good-names` default (i, j, k, ex, Run, _) was re-fetched but is not carried: Pylint's default snake_case regex `[^\W\dA-Z][^\WA-Z]*$` already accepts one-letter names, so the list is not an exemption in practice. The card lists no role for n: clang-tidy and clippy exempt n with no role, the Google TypeScript guide lists `n` as "Meaningless" among disallowed identifiers, and the Google C++ guide admits `int n = 0;` only with "limited scope and context", which the documented-tolerance condition covers. ESLint `id-length` (min 2, no default exceptions, flags a caught `e`) is not carried because it exempts no conventional letter by default. The EMSE 2019 extension of Hofmeister et al. (DOI 10.1007/s10664-018-9621-x, cited from memory) and Scanniello et al. 2017 (abbreviations, not letters) are not carried. Lambda and closure parameters are triggered by their arrow, bar, lambda-keyword and in-closure forms. The Lawrie and Beniamini abstracts are relayed by WebSearch summaries and match the GitHub-hosted IEEE metadata mirror; the Hofmeister full text is fetched from the authors' GitHub Pages repository.

The Rationale says look-alike identifiers "can render identically", not that they look alike in every font: the confusables skeleton also joins pairs a careful reader tells apart (m and rn, mathematical bold f and f). The card takes `triggers: []` and reads every hunk, because no added-line pattern marks two names one character apart. The Unicode clause reaches one file, the card's scope, though rustc compares a whole crate and clang-tidy a translation unit, and it covers pairs in which one identifier holds a non-ASCII character, as rustc's `confusable_idents` does. Checked by hand: clippy with `-W clippy::pedantic` and with `-W clippy::similar_names` flags the Example's `row_recs`/`row_reps` pair and raises no naming lint on the good half; clippy 1.94 with `-W clippy::similar_names` flags `splunk`/`splonk`, `checked_exp`/`checked_eap`, `orange`/`ornange`, `pos_x_max`/`pos_y_max`, `page1_total`/`page12_total`, `rows`/`rrows` and `lines`/`ilines`, and not `row`/`rows`, `page1`/`page2`, `pos_x`/`pos_y`, `x_pos`/`y_pos`, `lhs`/`rhs`, `iter`/`item`, `parsed`/`parser` or `args`/`arms`; rustc warns `confusable_idents` on a Latin/Cyrillic `total` pair; the good half compiles with rustc 1.94.1 --emit=metadata. Not carried: clang-tidy's comparison of all-ASCII pairs through the confusables skeleton (`comer`/`corner`, `row_ll`/`row_l1`), which rustc does not report; clippy's skip of `#[test]` functions, of names containing an uppercase letter and of names beginning with an underscore (Rust conventions, not the misreading mechanism); rustc's `mixed_script_confusables` and `uncommon_codepoints` single-identifier lints; the type-parameter case, which the letter-check sources do not name, so Limits bounds it out. SonarSource's RSPEC-1479 text for Java, Go, PHP, JavaScript and Kotlin calls a switch with a large set of cases usually an attempt to map two sets of data and asks for a map. Its C# and VB.NET rule reports a switch above the same thirty only when a case clause holds more than one statement. Its text holds that a switch whose case clauses are all single-line keeps its readability, and it fixes a multi-line clause by extracting it into a method, which leaves a switch whose cases each return a value or call one routine. No fetched source separates the two positions, so the card leaves every switch and match outside the rule and states both positions in its Limits. Ruff classes its own SIM116 as pedantic ("highly opinionated or prone to false positives"); the card names that classification in its Limits as a project tolerance. · notes: confidence moderate. The evidence is a standard's description with no threshold (SWEBOK §4.7) and one tool rule written for one language (Ruff SIM116), bounded below by PMD TooFewBranchesForSwitch; the two RSPEC-1479 texts are cited for the Limits only. No study measuring table-driven code against conditional chains was found: the topic's search of the neverworkintheory and papers-we-love bibliographies found none, Vessey and Weber (CACM 29(1), 1986) and Pooch, "Translation of decision tables" (ACM Computing Surveys 6(2), 1974) could not be opened, and Harel (1987) and Heninger (1980) concern statecharts and requirements tables, not this claim. WebSearch was unavailable in this run. The three-branch count is a tool default and comes from a Python rule. Not carried, for want of a separating condition: a switch, a match or an if/else-if chain of more than thirty non-empty cases over a non-enumerated key, and a table of routines for a selection whose cases each call one routine. They rested on the Java and Go text of RSPEC-1479 and on two Python sources, the Design and History FAQ, "Why isn't there a switch or case statement in Python?" ("For cases where you need to choose from a very large number of possibilities, you can create a dictionary mapping case values to functions to call."; fetched from `python/cpython` main, `Doc/faq/design.rst`) and PEP 275 "Switching on Multiple Values" (2001, Rejected), §Problem ("This works well for state machines which require complex and lengthy processing in the different case methods. It does not perform well for ones which only process one or two instructions per case"; fetched from `python/peps` main, `peps/pep-0275.rst`); the C# and VB.NET text of RSPEC-1479 contests both. Not carried either: Code Complete's direct, indexed and stair-step access (formulation only). Range lookup, table-miss handling and closing a handler table against reflective dispatch are other rules of the topic. The Java example's good half compiles with javac 21 under `import java.util.Map`. The triggers keep the research spine's two chain patterns, the first without its end anchor, and add string-equality chains; the spine's case and match-arm patterns go with the thirty-case clause.

The run-time failures the card carries are the two that depend on reach (the member reached is not a function; an inherited standard method is called with the wrong arguments); the failure on a name with no entry, which the qhelp also names, is not carried, because the forms the card accepts (a closed table, a fixed prefix) also fail on such a name and its handling is left out of the rule. The validator passes an own-entry check only on a table that holds only the handlers, as the CodeQL help ("At the very least, check that the method is an own property") allows for its `actions` table. It does not pass one on the global object, a module namespace or a general object: for the global object the CodeQL `js/unsafe-dynamic-method-access` help gives only an allowlist or a change of the object the methods are stored on, the Semgrep `dangerous-globals-use` rule has no exemption for a membership check, and `eval` and `Function` are own properties of the global object (checked in Node 21). The Semgrep `unsafe-dynamic-method` exemption, which accepts a `hasOwnProperty` guard on any object, is not followed there. Scope kept to the selection of a method or function: class instantiation by a computed name (`Class.forName`), the pattern of the Semgrep `unsafe-reflection` rule itself, is stated in the Limits as outside the rule and is not triggered or judged, although that rule's message covers method invocation too. The prefix allowance rests on the FAQ's statement about methods on one object and is not extended to a module or global namespace, where the sources give an allowlist, a map or code that stops indexing the namespace; the getattr, getMethod and MethodByName triggers skip only a name argument that is a whole string literal, and the getattr trigger accepts a subscripted first argument such as sys.modules[__name__], so a prefixed name and a lookup among the current module's functions still reach the finder. The finder works at scope hunk, so a key whose untrusted origin the hunk does not show is not flagged. The table's default entry and the handling of a missing key are left out of the rule. In a language with no lookup of a member by a runtime name only the table form exists. Fetched but not cited: the OWASP www-community page "Unsafe use of Reflection" (a community wiki page outside the admissible classes; its command-dispatcher example shows a `Class.forName(ctl + "Command")` refactoring that "allows an attacker to instantiate any object that implements the Worker interface"), the experimental CodeQL `java/unsafe-reflection` query help, and eslint-plugin-security `detect-object-injection` (flags every bracket access and does not state the reach claim). Formulation: the topic's canon locator, Code Complete 2nd ed. §18.1 (a table entry that stores a reference to the routine implementing the action; unfetched), is not named as the formulation because the openable FAQ carries the same formulation; R. Pike, "Notes on Programming in C" §"Function pointers" was not opened from this environment and is not named either

Nichols, The Rust Programming Language, ch. 18.3 "Implementing an Object-Oriented Design Pattern": requirements "A blog post starts as an empty draft." and "Only published blog posts return content to print so that unapproved posts can’t accidentally be published."; "Any other changes attempted on a post should have no effect. For example, if we try to approve a draft blog post before we’ve requested a review, the post should remain an unpublished draft."; "we call an internal `request_review` method on the current state of `Post`, and this second `request_review` method consumes the current state and returns a new state"; "when we request a review on a post already in the `PendingReview` state, it should stay in the `PendingReview` state"; "if we call the `approve` method on a `Draft`, it will have no effect because `approve` will return `self`"; "we might instead use `match` expressions in the methods on `Post` or even in the `main` code that checks the state of the post and changes behavior in those places"; § Encoding States and Behavior as Types: "Rather than encapsulating the states and transitions completely so that outside code has no knowledge of them, we’ll encode the states into different types. (fetched from `rust-lang/book` main, `src/ch18-03-oo-design-patterns.md`). The Embedded Rust Book, Static Guarantees: "Peripherals as State Machines": "this would allow us to modify certain registers that do not make sense. For some hardware, this may not matter. On other hardware, it could cause unexpected or undefined behavior!"; "Although this interface is convenient to write, it doesn't enforce the design contracts set out by our hardware implementation."; "Design Contracts": "If we instead checked the state before making use of the underlying hardware, enforcing our design contracts at runtime", with setters that `return Err(());` under the comments "Must be enabled to set direction", "Must be enabled to set input mode", "Direction must be input" and "Direction must be output" before `self.periph.modify(...)`, while `set_enable` carries no check; "Because we need to enforce the restrictions on the hardware, we end up doing a lot of runtime checking which wastes time and resources, and this code will be much less pleasant for the developer to use."; § Compile Time Functional Safety: "Because we are enforcing our design constraints entirely at compile time, this incurs no runtime cost."; "there is no runtime penalty due to checking the current state before executing a function"; "If they try to perform an illegal state transition, the code will not compile!" (fetched from `rust-embedded/book` master, `src/static-guarantees/state-machines.md` and `design-contracts.md`). Hands-on, not cited in the card: javac 21.0.10 with `-Xlint:all` compiles the Example's good half without warnings inside `class Order { enum Status { IN_PROGRESS, PAID, SHIPPED } private Status status = Status.IN_PROGRESS; ... }`; run, it refuses `ship()` in IN_PROGRESS ("cannot ship an order in state IN_PROGRESS", status unchanged) and in SHIPPED, and ships after `pay()`, while the bad half ships an unpaid order (local run under /tmp/craft-research; not openable until committed under the skill's `evals/fixture/`). · topic: table-driven-and-state-machines (research/software-craft/table-driven-and-state-machines.md) · formulation: N. Nilsson, "Thinking in States", 97 Things Every Programmer Should Know, thing 84, the paragraph after the order's three states ("These states are important and you need to check that you're in the expected state before doing operations, and that you only move to a legal state from where you are. In short, you have to protect your objects carefully, in the right places.") and final paragraph ("If your state is incorrect, there's a bug and you risk trashing data if you don't abort.") (opened from `97-things/97-things-every-programmer-should-know` master, `en/thing_84/README.md`); D. Thomas and A. Hunt, The Pragmatic Programmer 20th anniv. ed., Topic 29 (an event with no entry in the transition table moves the machine to an explicit error state; not opened); S. Wlaschin, "Designing with types: Making state explicit" (2013), state-by-event table with disallowed cells marked n/a (not opened) · reception: not contested · notes: confidence moderate. The evidence is documentation, not measurement: standard libraries of Java, Python and Go refuse an operation the current state does not allow, by an exception, a panic or a false result; the Rust book's workflow specifies documented no-ops for its illegal pairs and shows dispatch to the current state's handler and branching on the state as the two run-time forms of the check; the Embedded Rust Book shows unchecked setters reaching states the machine does not define, with "unexpected or undefined behavior" on some hardware only, the run-time check returning an error, and the type-encoded alternative. No study measuring defects from unchecked state changes was found (WebSearch budget exhausted; no GitHub-hosted paper located). The card's title says "refused" where the spine said "refused with an error", since the evidence also shows a refusal reported by a returned result (`Future.cancel` returning False, the GPIO setters returning `Err(())`). The concurrent.futures `Future` is a type shared between threads; it is cited only for its refusal semantics, and the card keeps thread-shared state machines out of scope. The rule every-state-event-pair-decided is folded into the Thesis's third sentence. Not carried as claims: the Pragmatic Programmer's error state for an unlisted event (unopened); what a transition-table lookup yields for a pair without an entry, owned by the table-miss card and present here only as a Validator check; an object found in an impossible state, owned by ERR-06 and named in the Limits only as excluded scope; the last Limits sentence is the topic's ownership scope, not an evidence claim. The type-encoded form is described in the Limits without naming a language and is conditioned on the transition consuming the old state's value, as the Rust book states, since a language that lets a caller keep the old state's value keeps the illegal call possible. Triggers: one pattern, an assignment to a name ending in state, status, phase or stage (receiver-qualified or bare), which matches the Example's bad half.

the card's Example good half compiles, runs, and type-checks clean under both · topic: table-driven-and-state-machines (research/software-craft/table-driven-and-state-machines.md) · formulation: Error Prone MissingCasesInEnumSwitch ("Switches on enum types should either handle all values, or have a default case") and typescript-eslint switch-exhaustiveness-check ("if the union type or the enum changes, it's easy to forget to modify the cases to account for any new types"), cited above, whose wording the Thesis and Rationale follow (openable) · reception: not contested. Tool defaults differ on whether a default branch stands in for a named member. typescript-eslint (considerDefaultExhaustiveForUnions false) and exhaustive (without -d) still report a missing member when a default is present. Error Prone MissingCasesInEnumSwitch, PMD NonExhaustiveSwitch and the Google Java Style Guide accept a default. The anchors are three Java checks or style rules, one TypeScript and one Go checker, and the language specifications and official documentation of Python, Go, TypeScript, Rust and Java for which constructs fall out silently and which are compiler-checked. They document the practice and its reason; no empirical study measures failures from a missing member. Error Prone is WARNING severity; typescript-eslint's rule needs type information and is in neither the recommended nor the strict preset. The Go FAQ entry on variant types was dropped because it says nothing about switch exhaustiveness. The Go claim that a named integer type can hold values outside its constants (hands-on label(State(42)) = "?") was also dropped: only the unopenable local check states it, and it bears on whether a fully covered switch keeps a default, which another rule of the topic owns. What a default does with a value believed impossible, and whether a default on an already-exhaustive switch is kept, are left to their own cards. A table or map lookup that misses a member (hands-on: a Go map and a Java EnumMap return the zero value or null) belongs to the topic's table-completeness rule.

The clause should either take appropriate action, or contain a suitable comment as to why no action is taken."; sonar-java Exceptions: "If the switch parameter is an Enum and if all the constants of this enum are used in the case statements, then no default clause is expected." · Error Prone BuiltInCheckerSuppliers (google/error-prone master, `core/src/main/java/com/google/errorprone/scanner/BuiltInCheckerSuppliers.java`, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/google/error-prone/master/core/src/main/java/com/google/errorprone/scanner/BuiltInCheckerSuppliers.java), fetched, reception only — `MissingCasesInEnumSwitch.class` is listed in ENABLED_WARNINGS and `UnnecessaryDefaultInEnumSwitch.class` in DISABLED_CHECKS · topic: table-driven-and-state-machines (research/software-craft/table-driven-and-state-machines.md) · formulation: Error Prone MissingCasesInEnumSwitch, "This could be made clear by adding: `default: throw new AssertionError(color);`" (fetched, cited above), the raising default the card keeps where an unknown value can reach the switch · reception: contested. One side wants a default in every switch: Checkstyle MissingSwitchDefault, the Google TypeScript Style Guide, and SonarSource S131 for Go, which has no enumeration exception. The other side wants no catch-all default on a checked exhaustive switch: Error Prone UnnecessaryDefaultInEnumSwitch, typescript-eslint switch-exhaustiveness-check with allowDefaultCaseForExhaustiveSwitch: false, and rust-clippy wildcard_enum_match_arm. The Google C++ Style Guide states neither position: it exempts a switch on an enumerated value from its default requirement because the compiler warns about unhandled values, and asks that a default that should never execute be treated as an error. Every tool rule on the no-default side is opt-in: UnnecessaryDefaultInEnumSwitch is among Error Prone's disabled checks, allowDefaultCaseForExhaustiveSwitch defaults to true, and clippy's two lints are restriction and pedantic. The separating condition is whether a value outside the compiled-against members can reach the switch at run time. It is sourced in Error Prone's 'When the default can be removed' and 'Library skew', typescript-eslint's allowDefaultCaseForExhaustiveSwitch Caveats, the Rust Reference's non_exhaustive attribute and the mypy documentation. Checkstyle MissingSwitchDefault and sonar-java S131 themselves exempt compiler-checked switch expressions and pattern switches, and enum switches that use every constant · notes: confidence moderate. Static-analysis rule pages, language documentation and style guides agree on the mechanism, and no source measures a defect rate. The binary-compatibility argument is Java's (the Error Prone page cites JLS §13.4.26, **unfetched**, docs.oracle.com denied), so the card states it conditionally ("where adding a member does not force dependent code to be recompiled") and asks, for the library case, that the dependency can be upgraded beneath the switch without its exhaustiveness being checked again. The fall-through precondition and the no-report case for a default whose removal breaks compilation are Error Prone's own; the Rationale's exception for a language that raises on an unmatched value rests on the MatchException Javadoc (JLS §14.11.3 and §15.28.2, which it cites, **unfetched**). Step is implement and refactor: the rule concerns code inside a switch, not the shape of the change. Hands-on checks, none a card anchor: tsc 6.0.2 --strict compiles the Example's good half inside `function weight(state: "open" | "closed"): number` and fails it with TS2366 once a third member is added, while the bad half compiles silently in both versions; the good half protects only where the function declares its return type. javac/java 21: with a Lib compiled against `Color { RED, GREEN }` and run with BLUE added, the statement switch fell out and returned -1 while the default-less switch expression threw java.lang.MatchException; an enum switch whose cases all return draws "missing return statement" and compiles with `throw new AssertionError(s);` after it; a case falling into the default gave 12 with the default and 2 once it was removed. go vet reports "missing return" for the same Go switch over iota constants. rustc 1.94.1 warns "unreachable pattern" on a `_` arm after every variant of a local enum; the skeptic's rustc 1.97.0 run (not repeated here) showed that a Rust library built against one version of a dependency does not link with a newer one (E0460) and that recompiling reports the uncovered variant (E0004). The TypeScript handbook's never default returns rather than raises, so the card's raising form rests on typing.assert_never, Error Prone MissingCasesInEnumSwitch and the Google C++ guide. non_exhaustive_omitted_patterns is allow-by-default and feature-gated, which is why the card does not flag a counted wildcard that the language forces where no check sees through it. The Go exhaustive analyzer is a third-party tool, cited for the Go mechanism only. The card does not carry a default that deliberately groups members a switch leaves unnamed, because tool defaults split on it: Error Prone MissingCasesInEnumSwitch and rustc accept it, typescript-eslint by default and the exhaustive analyzer report it, and clippy reports it only in restriction and pedantic. Nor does it carry the default, fallthrough and form of a switch over a non-enumerated value, which belong to control flow

Not carried: the original wording's demand that the comment name each participating type's role (the fetched abstracts state that the patterns, or the pattern instances, were documented in source comments, and none states what the comment said beyond that), so the card asks for the pattern's name only; nor does any abstract state where the comments stood, so the Thesis and the Validator accept a comment elsewhere in the file that names the pattern and lists the type as a participant; the formulation's participant-name convention (TeXLayoutStrategy) is carried only as the Limits' boundary — the two-experiment study contrasted pattern comment lines with a well-commented program without explicit reference to design patterns, and the four-experiment abstract does not describe its control code, so the boundary rests on the first study and a declaration that names the pattern lies outside its measured contrast — and not as a disclosure the evidence validated; whether a pattern fits its problem, and the reception's pattern-versus-simpler-solution question, belong to the topic's other rules. Step: `implement`, `refactor` and `document` — the rule applies when code that implements a pattern is added, a refactoring that introduces a pattern included; `review` is reserved for the shape and description of the change. Triggers: the orchestrator's `(self|this)[.]` forwarding-field pattern was widened to `[.]` so that a Go receiver (`s.inner`) also dispatches, and the type-name suffixes were extended with the remaining structural and behavioral catalogue names (Composite, Facade, Mediator, Bridge, Prototype, Flyweight, Memento); the routine-name patterns accept an initial capital (exported Go names) and a cls parameter, and the forwarding-field pattern an underscore prefix and the adaptee field name.

The linter counts govern the total or positional arguments of any routine; the card reports them as documented counts and keeps the TypeScript guide's "more than a small handful of optional parameters that do not have a natural order" as its condition, which it reads as five or more optional inputs taken by position: beside even one required input the signature then exceeds Pylint R0917's default of more than five positional arguments (a method's first parameter not counted: `if node.type in {"method", "classmethod"}: pos_args = pos_args[1:]`), while clippy's more than seven and PMD's ten or more count every parameter of any routine and do not raise that bar; R0913 also counts keyword-only parameters (`args = pos_args + node.args.kwonlyargs`), so it flags the good half as well and supports only the Rationale's general-count sentence. The Uber guide's count of three or more arguments, and the original wording's per-language mapping (keyword parameters in Python, a destructured options object in TypeScript, an option struct in Go, a builder in Rust or Java "which have no named or default arguments") are not carried: the card names no language, and the claim that Rust and Java lack named or default arguments rests only on formulation sources, so the card lists the named forms without tying them to languages. The Go guide's "consider" and the TypeScript guide's "prefer" are recommendation-strength; the card states the rule at minor severity and carries "may be unnecessary" for unexported constructors in Limits. `step` is design, implement and refactor: `review` is reserved for the shape and description of the change itself, and replacing positional optional inputs or a telescoping family with a named form changes structure while keeping behaviour. The card's scope is constructors and factories by topic ownership; long parameter lists of other routines, a method that configures an existing value among them, are left to the routine-shape topic. The TypeScript constructor trigger is widened from optional markers to default initializers. Example: the good half runs with python3 3.13 inside `class Client:`, and the bad call `Client("db", 5432, 30.0, 3, True)` raises TypeError ("takes 2 positional arguments but 6 were given") against it, as Pylint's R0917 good example states for a keyword-only signature; the bad half takes five optional inputs by position, the card's bar

(fetched from `cmu-sei/secure-coding-standards` main, `content/6.sei-cert-oracle-coding-standard-for-java/3.rules/12.miscellaneous-msc/09.msc07-j.md`). · topic: design-patterns-in-construction (research/software-craft/design-patterns-in-construction.md) · formulation: Google TypeScript Style Guide "Container classes" (also cited in the card as official documentation); PMD `InstantiableUtilityClass` naming history (known as `UseSingleton` before PMD 5.1.0), the pattern framing that places the rule in this topic · reception: contested. SEI CERT MSC07-J (draft) counts classes with only static methods as good Singleton candidates. The Google Guice wiki holds that static state is what hurts and that static classes are fine, even preferred, for pure functions. typescript-eslint, the Google TypeScript and Python style guides, Checkstyle, PMD and SonarSource S1118 hold that a namespace class is unnecessary where modules exist and that a utility class should not be instantiable. The card's separating condition is state. CERT's sentence is unconditional on its own, so the card reads it within its paragraph, whose subject is a single instance whose fields occur once like static fields and which often controls a resource such as a database connection or socket. Guice's split between static state and the static keyword is the sourced side of the condition. · notes: confidence moderate. The evidence is analyzer documentation from four tools (one for TypeScript, three for Java), two official style guides (TypeScript, Python) and the TypeScript handbook, plus a framework wiki and a draft CERT rule for the contest; no empirical study of the cost is carried. The card narrows the tools' reach. Checkstyle, PMD and SonarSource also flag classes whose static fields hold mutable state, but the card reaches only a type whose static fields hold constants. It leaves static mutable state and resource-holding singletons to variables-scope-and-numerics, following the topic's ownership note. typescript-eslint's reasons about IDE suggestions and dead-code analysis ("IDEs can't provide as good suggestions for static class or namespace imported properties…", "It's more difficult to statically analyze code for unused variables, etc. when they're all on the class") are not carried, because they describe JavaScript and TypeScript tooling. The rule's original statement said Go and Rust meet the rule by construction. The card drops that sentence: a fieldless Rust struct whose associated functions take no receiver is the same namespace-only type, and the Rust example shows it. No Rust- or Go-specific source was found, so the reach to Rust rests on the module mechanism the TypeScript and Python sources describe, and the card states this as a caveat. Go has no static members, so the rule does not arise there. The Rationale's statement that a compiler-generated constructor takes the class's own access, and the Validator's skip of every enumeration where every function must belong to a class, rest on the compiler, because SonarSource's "implicitly generating a public parameterless constructor" holds only for a public class: OpenJDK javac sets a generated constructor's flags with `flags = (owner().flags() & AccessFlags) | GENERATEDCONSTR;` and comments "constructors of true enums are private" (fetched from `openjdk/jdk` master, `src/jdk.compiler/share/classes/com/sun/tools/javac/comp/TypeEnter.java`), and javap 21 shows `p.StringUtils();` for a package-private class, `private p.Outer$Helpers();` for a private nested class and `private p.HttpConstants();` for an enum. The card leaves out a type with no members, an enumeration that declares a value and a private class that declares no constructor, as the analyzers do: PMD `InstantiableUtilityClassRule` visits class declarations only and counts the default constructor only on a class that is not private, and SonarSource `UtilityClassWithPublicConstructorCheck` visits classes only and skips a private inner class (both fetched from `pmd/pmd` main and `SonarSource/sonar-java` master). Severity is minor, following the design facet, even though SonarSource defaults to Major: the evidence names a clarity cost, not a measured one. The triggers are two patterns, each spanning the languages: declarations (the class-name pattern with widened modifiers and the `struct` and `enum` keywords, a final class, a Rust unit or empty struct) and members (a static member, a static-method decorator, a private parameterless constructor, a Rust `pub` associated function without a receiver or associated constant). The private-parameterless-constructor alternative fires on Java classes that already comply, so the finder answers no unless a public constructor remains. Closing edits from the final skeptic verdict: the title says "hides its constructor", following Checkstyle's word "hide", because a protected or package-private constructor, which the Thesis and Validator accept, still leaves the class instantiable within its package or through a subclass (javac 21 reproduction). The skip of abstract types applies only where every function must belong to a class: that exclusion comes from the Java analyzers (PMD's "concrete class" criterion, Checkstyle's early return), while typescript-eslint's test suite lists `abstract class Foo { static property: string; }` as invalid (fetched from `packages/eslint-plugin/tests/rules/no-extraneous-class.test.ts`, main). The Thesis's statement that a private constructor can be called from a type that encloses the class rests on the compiler: javac 21 compiles `new Hidden()` inside `Outer` against `Hidden`'s private constructor (exit 0). The fix splits as SonarSource's `UtilityClassWithPublicConstructorCheck` does ("Hide this public constructor." / "Add a private constructor to hide the implicit public one.").

Scope of the evidence: Sonar and Error Prone check Java anonymous classes only; Pylint flags any class with fewer than 2 public methods whatever its fields, which the card narrows to classes with no field changing between calls, following Sonar's and Error Prone's single-member condition; Sonar's `useThisInstance` and Object-superclass conditions are written for a Java anonymous class, which its check accepts only without fields, and a Java lambda converts only to an interface, so the card carries them as a use of the instance beyond reading its fields and a base class that declares more than the one abstract operation, the classes Pylint R0903 still reports (pylint 4.1.2 on a probe reports a one-method ABC, its stateless subclass, a subclass reading a constructor-set field and a `__call__` class); an operation with its own type parameters is excluded following the check's `.filter(symbol -> !symbol.isParametrizedMethod())` (sonar-java java-frontend/src/main/java/org/sonar/plugins/java/api/semantic/Symbol.java, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SonarSource/sonar-java/master/java-frontend/src/main/java/org/sonar/plugins/java/api/semantic/Symbol.java, fetched — '@return true if the method has type parameters.'). javac 21 rejects a lambda for `interface Mapper { <T> T map(Object o); }` ('invalid functional descriptor for lambda expression ... is generic'), and tsc accepts a generic arrow function for `type Mapper = <T>(x: T) => T`; the exemption for a class a library exports for its users rests on Uber's 'test for users' and on Error Prone's `canBeRemoved` restriction to code not accessible outside its compilation unit; typescript-eslint concerns the type declaration (a single call signature), not an implementing class, and sits in the stylistic config; Effective Go shows the adapter but names no condition. The card does not carry GoF's undo, queueing and logging as named conditions (book, formulation only); it carries their sourced counterparts: a second operation, a changing field, a comparison, a string form, identity. Prechelt, Unger, Tichy, Brössler, Votta, IEEE TSE 27(12) 2001 (**relayed** by the orchestrator's search: "positive effects from using a design pattern" in most of nine maintenance tasks) and its replications, Vokáč et al. EMSE 9(3) 2004 (**relayed**) and Krein et al. RESER 2011 (**relayed**), compare pattern-based designs with simpler solutions and say nothing about function-value forms, so they are not carried. The card's title rewords the orchestrator's draft title ("rather than as a one-method interface with a class implementing it") because the single-operation interface stays as the function value's type in several languages; the defect is the implementing class. Ownership: a singleton used as a global goes to variables-scope-and-numerics, the inheritance a pattern rests on to inheritance-versus-composition, and pipelines and higher-order functions to functional-style-and-pipelines. The scope is `callers` because the test or mock that compares the value usually sits in a separate test file. The triggers are broad by design: an execute/perform/invoke call and the Java functional-interface names dispatch a finder whose Validator exempts non-strategy uses. A Python subclass of a strategy-family base, a Go empty struct type and a Rust unit struct are reached through the sixth pattern; another Go method or Rust impl is reached only when a name on its line carries a strategy-family suffix. The Java example's good half was compiled with javac 21 against a stub DiscountPolicy interface and checkout routine.

Not carried: the hands-on run of this research round (rustc 1.94.1 E0004 non-exhaustive patterns; javac 21.0.10 "the switch expression does not cover all possible input values"; tsc 6.0.2 --strict TS2322 not assignable to never; go 1.24.7 go vet exit 0 and the unhandled variant silently returning 0; Python 3.11.15 match returning None), plus the drafters' mypy 1.19.1 / pyright 1.1.408 and, at revision, mypy 2.3.1 --strict / pyright 1.1.414 runs on the Example's good half (Python 3.13.16: compiles, both checkers pass; with a third variant added to the Shape alias, both report Triangle not assignable to Never), and the skeptic's reproduction that a void operation with no catch-all arm that misses a third variant passes tsc 6.0.2 --strict, mypy --strict and pyright at default settings while javac 21.0.12 and rustc 1.97.0 reject it — local scratch only, citable once committed under evals/fixture/. That reproduction is why the card asks for a final arm that asserts the matched value has no variant left, which the checker reports as an error once a variant can reach it, and allows a match with no catch-all arm only where the compiler or the project's checker reports every match that leaves a variant unhandled. Also not carried: Prechelt et al., IEEE TSE 27(12) 2001, and Krein et al., RESER 2011, both **relayed** and about patterns versus simpler solutions in general, not Visitor versus a match; the GoF footnote on double dispatch (formulation only). Trigger 3 was broadened from the research facet (adds impl, implements and extends, so `class Evaluator implements NodeVisitor<T>` and `impl Visitor for X` match); it is a superset of the original. Scope is `callers`, not `file`: a new visitor class often sits in its own file, and the Validator searches the repository for the set's declaration and the variants' accept methods. Ownership: the inheritance a visitor rests on → inheritance-versus-composition; a state machine dispatched by a match → table-driven-and-state-machines; pipelines over variants → functional-style-and-pipelines.

The paper's abstract says developers recognized "more than 75%" of the instances and its RQ3 summary says 71% (17 of 24); the card carries the RQ3 figure. The exclusion of renames, mechanical migrations and dependency upgrades is a scope bound drawn from the Thesis's condition (a change made for one requirement), not from a source.

The mechanism (refusal by toolchains, load-time failure where cycles are accepted, the linters' treatment of type-only, deferred, dynamic and self imports) rests on fetched specifications, official guides and tool rules; the defect association rests on two correlational studies, one fetched only through its abstract and a review, one relayed, and neither isolates cycles from other coupling. The anti-pattern study measures six anti-patterns together, with unstable interfaces and crossings contributing most by far. The research note defines MacCormack and Sturtevant's Core as the largest cyclic group of files, but that is the note's commentary, not a quotation, so the quoted core figures do not tie defects to cycles and the card does not carry them. Verified hands-on: rustc 1.97.0 (editions 2018, 2021 and 2024, --crate-type lib --emit=metadata, each elision given the body `let _ = o.total;`) compiles both halves of the card's Example, so a two-module import cycle inside one crate is accepted by the compiler, which is why the Example shows a cycle no build refuses; pylint 4.1.2 reports "R0401: Cyclic import (pkg.a -> pkg.b)" when pkg/b.py closes the cycle with "from pkg import a" inside a function and reports nothing when that import sits under "if TYPE_CHECKING:"; import-linter 2.15 reports an acyclic_siblings contract BROKEN ("- .green -> .blue (1 import)") on a sibling cycle closed by a guarded import by default, and KEPT with exclude_type_checking_imports = True. The card leaves out the formulation's claim that a cycle fuses its members into one unit that must be understood, tested and released together: only the talk and the books state it, and they are formulation only. The card's nearest evidence is the relayed abstract's background sentence on understandability, testability, reusability, buildability and maintainability. The card also leaves out the draft's per-language list of which toolchains accept cycles: the card names no language, and no fetched fragment states that list for every language. The title is restated positively from the draft wording ("does not close a cycle"). Package-level cycles are checked only where the project's configured cycle check declares sibling packages acyclic, as an import-linter acyclic_siblings contract does. The subtree semantics rest on that one opt-in Python contract. Verified hands-on: the Go 1.24.7 standard library, whose package graph the spec keeps acyclic, links sibling directories both ways (go/build/read.go imports go/parser while go/parser/parser.go imports go/build/constraint; crypto/internal/fips140/aes/gcm/gcm_nonces.go imports crypto/internal/fips140/drbg while drbg/ctrdrbg.go imports crypto/internal/fips140/aes). Imports that only the type checker reads are outside the rule by the default of three cycle checks, and inside it where the project's build or configured cycle check counts them: import-linter counts guarded imports by default (docs/get_started/configure.md; src/importlinter/application/use_cases.py), and the Google Python guide's typing-smell sentence, with its build-system reason, covers guarded typing imports too. Ownership: removing an import through an interface the importing module declares is named here only as a way to break a cycle; a high-level policy depending on a low-level detail without a cycle belongs to the topic's dependency-direction rule.

the public discussion johnousterhout/aposd-vs-clean-code README.md, "Method Length" and "Method Length Summary" (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/johnousterhout/aposd-vs-clean-code/main/README.md, fetched: "It is certainly possible to over-decompose code. The implementation is not more deeply detailed than the interface."; "We agree that it is possible to over-decompose"; "We disagree on how far to decompose"); Refactoring, 2nd ed., ch. 3 smell "Lazy Element" (**unfetched**); Clean Code ch. 3 "Functions" and ch. 10 "Classes" as the opposing formulation (**unfetched**) · reception: contested. Extract small named units: Robert C. Martin (Clean Code chs. 3 and 10; README "Method Length": "if I must err, I'd rather err on the side of decomposition. [...] They can always be inlined if we judge them to have gone too far."), Code Complete 2nd ed. §7.1 (**unfetched**), and on the tool side SonarSource S3776 "Method calls are free". A unit that hides nothing costs an interface: John Ousterhout (APOSD §4.5-4.6; README), the Google Go, TypeScript and Python style guides, typescript-eslint `no-extraneous-class`. Both authors accept the extreme case in the README (Martin calls the one-call `doSomething` over-decomposed and the one-line clearAmountOwed extraction not meaningful). The card separates the cases on whether the unit's body says more than its name and signature: a summary of multiple lines, which the decomposition side defends, against one call on the unit's own parameters or a class of only static members, which the depth side flags; how far to split a longer routine stays open · notes: confidence moderate. Every anchor is a tool rule or an official style guide, none a measurement, so the card carries no number. The forwarding test is documented by Pylint and clippy for lambdas and closures; the card applies it to named routines by the same mechanism (a body that is a call on the same argument list), with the Go guide's "unnecessary levels of abstraction" as the general statement, and the Source caveat says so. Because a named routine can be reached in ways a closure cannot, the card also exempts routines that a subclass overrides or a test replaces, routines that a decorator, annotation or attribute wraps or registers, and entry points a runtime, framework or test runner calls by name (clippy's own `#[track_caller]` exclusion is the closure-side analogue), and it does not count a receiver the routine declares; a routine that calls an operation on an object its own instance holds is outside the forwarding case, the method PMD `LawOfDemeter` recommends adding in place of `b.getC().doIt()`. The card's opening claim admits a single step, computation or decision as what a unit hides, following S3776's extraction of one condition into a named function. The namespace-class half rests on TypeScript and Python sources and on the TS rule's own reason ("already organized by virtue of being in a module"), so the card restricts it to languages with module-level functions and to types that extend or implement no other (a type implementing an interface or trait is used for dispatch, not as a namespace), and leaves static utility classes in languages without module-level functions outside; the Java example therefore shows the forwarding case. The TS rule's IDE-suggestion and unused-detection reasons are quoted in the Source but not carried into the Rationale, since they describe TypeScript tooling and rustc (checked with rustc on a scratch file) warns on an unused associated function as it does on an unused free function. The candidate papers (Chidamber and Kemerer 1994; Briand, Daly and Wüst 1998, DOI 10.1023/A:1009783721306; Olbrich, Cruzes and Sjøberg 2010; Muñoz Barón, Wyrich and Wagner 2020, arXiv:2007.12520; the JSS and EMSE understandability studies) measure class size, cohesion, God and Brain Classes or cognitive complexity, not a forwarding routine or a namespace class, so they do not state this rule's claim and are not carried. The size-count rules (PMD GodClass, ExcessivePublicCount, TooManyMethods; Pylint too-many-public-methods, too-few-public-methods) count members rather than test whether a unit hides anything and are not carried. The README and APOSD give the wording only. Overrides whose body only calls the inherited version are left to the inheritance topic, and how far to split a longer routine goes to routine-size-and-parameters.

Scope: the card carries only the narrow case where tools converge — an override, a class's only constructor or an embedded-field forward to the parent's same member with unchanged parameters; the formulation's broader pass-through method (a method that forwards to a method of another class with a similar signature) and the "different layer, different abstraction" claim are not carried, since no openable source separates a useful delegating method from a useless one. Departures from the statement as handed in: "an annotation or decorator that a framework reads" became any annotation or decorator other than the override marker or a warning suppression, which is what PMD implements (Sonar's check also lets a warning suppression clear it, Pylint any decorator, ESLint any parameter decorator); "widens or narrows visibility" became a visibility different from the parent's member or, for a constructor, from the constructor the class receives when it declares none (PMD UnnecessaryConstructor), a constructor marked non-public (narrowing being sourced for constructors only: ESLint, typescript-eslint), or a protected-style visibility redeclared in a package other than the parent's (PMD `isProtectedElevatingVisibility`); the constructor clause is conditioned on the language giving a class that declares no constructor one that delegates to the parent's (ESLint's stated premise) and on the constructor being the class's only one, with the implicit constructor's visibility and declared exceptions (PMD UnnecessaryConstructor), so a forwarding constructor in a language whose implicit constructor does not delegate is outside the rule — no openable language-specification statement on constructor inheritance was fetched, and the Limits state this as the converse of the Thesis condition; the declared-exception-list exemption is sourced for constructors only (PMD UnnecessaryConstructor's throws check) and no source states it for a method, where it only narrows what the rule flags; the abstract-member exemption rests on the CPython abc documentation and departs from Pylint W0246, which reports such an override although removing it makes the class impossible to instantiate; a parameter that declares a field (ESLint parameter property), the member-name skips — equals, hashCode and toString (Sonar), clone (PMD), `__hash__` next to `__eq__` (Pylint), each attributed in the Limits to one tool and taken together by the rule — and Sonar's transactional-class skip were added from the tools. The Go clause rests on Effective Go's statement that a promoted method has exactly the same effect as the forwarding method; no Go linter for it was found. The Validator's handling of a parent declared outside the file (constructor visibility keyword, default value, parameter decorator or field-declaring parameter clear the member; method visibility and types taken to match, except that a protected-style method clears it when its class extends a parent declared in another package) is a line the card draws from ESLint's file-local behaviour and PMD's other-package guard, not one a source states for methods. Trigger changes: the handed-in `^\s*super\s*\(` was broadened to `(?:^|[{;])\s*super\s*\(` so that a one-line constructor body matches, and the handed-in fifth trigger `^\s*(?:return\s+)?\w+[.][A-Z]\w*[.][A-Z]\w*\([^()]*\)\s*$` was broadened to `(?:^\s*|[{]\s*)(?:return\s+)?\w+[.][A-Z]\w*[.][A-Z]\w*\([^()]*\)\s*[}]?\s*$` so that a one-line forwarding method, which gofmt leaves on one line, matches; the fifth trigger targets a forward through a capitalized embedded field and misses lower-case embedded types. Checked by running: pylint 4.1.2 with its default configuration reports W0246 on an override of an abstract method that has a body, and CPython 3 then refuses to instantiate the class once the override is deleted. Not verified: RSPEC-1185's membership in the Sonar way profile (the profile path answered 404).

Item 2, required parameters in a builder's constructor; **unfetched**) and the same FSE 2015 study's default-value errors (17.5%–53.3% of configuration errors). The card resolves the dispute with the study's own separating condition. Parameters that are rarely set or set alike are defaulted or hidden (Finding 1(a), Guideline 1). The .NET 'Member Overloading' page prefers overloads to default arguments ("Default arguments are not CLS compliant"); that is a choice of mechanism, and the card leaves it open · notes: confidence moderate. The study's numbers come from configuration of system software set by its users and administrators (a commercial storage system, Apache httpd, MySQL, Hadoop); the paper itself limits its findings to "configuration design as the users' interface". The card carries those numbers to a module's code interface, where the Swift, Go, .NET and Rust guides and the IntelliJ inspection state the rule, each for its own language. No openable study measures defaults of code parameters. The Validator's 'more than half' is the plain reading of the Thesis's 'most' and narrows the Swift guideline's 'single commonly-used value'; it is not the study's 'majority (50+%)', which counts users whose settings differ from the default (§3.1, Fig. 3, Table 6), the parameters the study's Guideline 2 promotes to first-class knobs. The brief listed the FSE 2015 paper as relayed, but the full paper opened from the first author's GitHub Pages repository, so it is fetched. The security half of the .NET clause stays in the Thesis as a constraint on the default a fix chooses. The finding for an insecure default is left to a security corpus. Ownership: configuration files and their loading belong to runtime-configuration, and parameter count belongs to routine-size-and-parameters

Construction for reuse is usually based on variability analysis and design." The card separates the cases by a deliberate variability analysis for planned reuse, documented and tested, against a developer's speculation about the future. Tensions recorded and not carried: A Philosophy of Software Design ch. 6 (**unfetched**) recommends a somewhat general-purpose interface over functionality that reflects current needs, which the review guidance's "more generic than it needs to be" does not carve out; the position that mocks force abstractions, recorded in an openable exchange (johnousterhout/aposd-vs-clean-code, main, README.md, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/johnousterhout/aposd-vs-clean-code/main/README.md, fetched) — "Generally the decoupling arises because the test requires a mock of some kind. Mocks tend to force abstractions that might otherwise not exist." against "In my experience, mocking virtually never changes interfaces; it just provides replacements for existing (typically immovable) interfaces." — which the card's mock clause does not reach because it keeps the implementing-side scope that Go Code Review Comments gives it; the same 1983 paper's corollary "Use procedure arguments to provide flexibility in an interface" (fetched) endorses a hook as a means of flexibility, which the card leaves alone because it limits only hooks no present caller uses · notes: confidence moderate. The core claim (no abstraction, option or generality ahead of a present need) is stated directly by language-neutral review guidance and a peer-reviewed design paper. The five needs that justify an interface come from Go guidance written as "could"/"may"; the card carries them to abstract types and to the other four languages as design reasons and leaves out the Go-specific placement advice (the consumer defines the interface). The only figures are the 1983 paper's line counts for one system and an association study over 30 Java systems. That study's operationalization of speculative generality (an abstract class with fewer than three children using its methods) is broader than a single-implementation interface, and its authors read smells as co-occurring with fault-proneness, not causing it. Dropped from the orchestrator's wording: "a dependency whose direction must be inverted", because no fetched source states it. The Go guidance names only breaking a circular dependency between two packages, and a project context that fixes a layer's dependency direction rejects the finding instead. "A material need to substitute an implementation" is carried as a material need for a test double and as a returned type whose provider must stay replaceable without a breaking change, the two forms the guide states. The orchestrator's carve-out for keeping an interface general over existing functionality has no openable source and is not carried. The wrapper prohibition keeps the guide's generated-RPC scope; a project-owned wrapper around another third-party library, doubled in unit tests and run against the real library in integration tests, is carved out on the Mockito wiki's recommendation. An interface that only names the shape of a data value (a TypeScript object type) declares no behaviour for an implementation to supply and is outside the rule, since every source speaks of interfaces whose methods implementations supply. The last trigger also matches a Go variadic options parameter (`opts ...Option`). Type parameters (generics) are left to the code domain. Neither DOI was opened (doi.org denied); both are confirmed by the GitHub-hosted pages cited above, and the Palomba paper's journal, volume and pages come from the author page's BibTeX (fpalomba.github.io index.html, fetched).

the platform-variant case rests on the review's summary, not on the abstract; always-on card (triggers []), since an edit to one copy has no lexical or structural signature; the card does not carry the existence of duplicated blocks in a diff (the duplicate_block signal), duplicated knowledge across code, data and schemas, or derived data stored beside its source, which other rules of the topic own, nor the extraction mechanics, which belong to refactoring; the 97 Things exception for repetition that meets performance requirements (data denormalization) is a practitioner statement and is not carried

97 Things Every Programmer Should Know, thing 30 "Don't Repeat Yourself", 97-things/97-things-every-programmer-should-know en/thing_30/README.md (fetched, formulation only) — "to be certain that changes made in one location do not also need to be made in other places that duplicate the logic they are working on"; The Art of Unix Programming ch. 4 "The SPOT Rule" · reception: contested — for writing the repeated block once: Juergens et al. 2009, CWE-1041, PMD CPD, Pylint R0801, SonarSource S4144, SWEBOK V3 §3.5, Hermans and Aivaloglou 2016; for accepting a copy under named conditions: Kapser and Godfrey 2008 (boiler-plating, replicate and specialize, cross-cutting concerns, experimental forks), Rahman, Bird and Devanbu 2012 (clones not shown more defect-prone), PMD CPD (code that may never change), Google Go style decisions (duplication between test cases for readability); practitioner reception on the same side, not evidence: Metz "The Wrong Abstraction", Dahan "Beware the Share", Software Engineering at Google ch. 12 "DAMP, Not DRY", the Go proverb "A little copying is better than a little dependency", Abramov, Endler (none re-opened); the card states the rule where the copies are meant to do the same thing and so must change together, and carries the accepted cases in Limits with each side's evidence · notes: confidence moderate. The fault link rests on one large-scale case study's abstract (Juergens) and the modification cost on one controlled experiment with 61 novices in Scratch (Hermans); the change-cost mechanism rests on CWE-1041, the CPD documentation and official Rust documentation; the floors are detector defaults, not measured thresholds. The four-line floor is Pylint's, a Python checker that counts textually identical lines after dropping blank lines, comments, docstrings, imports and signatures; the card applies it across languages and to parameterized copies, where the multi-language detectors default higher (jscpd 5 lines and 50 tokens, dupl 100 tokens on its CLI and 150 under golangci-lint, CPD a required token count). The routine-level floor follows S4144's documented exception ("only one line of code"), not "two statements". Kapser and Godfrey's pattern verdicts and the experimental-fork case are read through the paper's abstract and its conclusion as quoted in a review, and the platform-variation and language-idiom kinds through the reviewer's summary; the case study covers two systems (the Apache web server and Gnumeric). The duplicate_block signal compares only the diff's own added lines, so a copy of code already in the repository reaches the finder only through a comment trigger or through the finder's search for an added routine's body; the card adds a "copy of / duplicate of" comment trigger to the planned four, and the Example's bad half carries two comments ("copied from total(); keep in sync" and "copy of total(): same steps as total()") so that each of the four comment triggers matches a bad-half line and none matches the good half. Not carried: Charalampidou et al., XP '17 Scientific Workshops, DOI 10.1145/3120459.3120465 (fetched abstract: "interest probability of code clones seems to be higher than the other two examined code smells"), a hedged workshop result on change-proneness that adds nothing the fetched anchors lack; SonarSource S1871 (fetched; identical branch bodies, one-line branches exempt), whose remedy is combining the conditions, not extracting a routine; SonarSource S1192, since a repeated literal belongs to the variables and numerics topic; Wagner et al. arXiv:1803.10542, Roy, Zibran and Koschke arXiv:2005.01005 and arXiv:2409.08555 (**unfetched**: arxiv.org denied, WebSearch budget spent), none anchoring the card; the Rahman MSR 2010 abstract (bird.bib) was not re-opened because the EMSE 2012 abstract carries the claim. Example language Rust; the good half compiled with rustc 1.97.0 (--edition 2021 --crate-type=lib --emit=metadata) in an Order impl.
