Both locators and quotations are carried from the topic research and were not re-opened in this run · reception: not contested · notes: confidence moderate. Four static-analysis checks (one of them documented for many languages, four of whose language rules are cited; RSPEC-1192 is also documented in sonar-php, sonar-kotlin, sonar-dotnet, sonar-ruby and sonar-scala) and one official language book agree on the remedy, a named constant in place of a repeated string literal; the SonarSource rules, goconst and the book name the mechanism, a change that must reach every occurrence, while Checkstyle says only that duplication makes maintenance more difficult and PMD names no mechanism. They disagree on the numbers (an occurrence floor from two to four, a length floor from one character (any non-empty literal) to ten characters) and on call arguments, which goconst leaves out by default under the linter runner while the SonarSource, PMD and Checkstyle checks count them, as the card does, so the card takes the three-occurrence and five-character defaults of the multi-language check and reports the others in its Rationale. No research is cited: none of the candidate clone studies (which cover code-block clones) states a claim about repeated literals, so none backs the card. Severity is minor although the SonarSource metadata rates the rule Critical with high maintainability impact, because no source ties repeated literals to failures or to a measured cost. The 'one purpose' condition narrows the tool rules to the case their own rationale names (a change propagated to all occurrences) and to the remedy two checks hedge ('can usually be improved', 'it can be better'); no tool implements it. The bare-word exclusion follows three of the four language rules of the SonarSource check. Its Java rule, PMD, Checkstyle and goconst count such literals. The sonar-python description's own noncompliant example ("action1", three times) contradicts its exception, and the implementation follows the exception. The existing-constant clause rests on the sonar-java implementation and goconst's match-constant default. Checkstyle and PMD state per-file counting, and the sonar-python, sonar-java, sonar-go and SonarJS rules implement it; goconst counts across a package. The card does not carry several things: the exclusions tied to one language's syntax (JSX attributes, require calls, object-literal property keys, type-level literals and member-access keys in the SonarJS rule; format patterns and colour codes in the sonar-python rule; arguments to fmt.Printf, Fprintf and Sprintf and redirect paths, which the sonar-go implementation leaves out and its description does not list); constants that duplicate one another's values (goconst find-duplicates, off by default); repeated numeric literals, which variables-scope-and-numerics owns; and knowledge duplicated across code, data and documentation, which other rules of the topic own.

It's better to make the length a calculated field"; the performance cache localized so that "only the methods within the class have to worry about keeping things straight", each setter recalculating the length; read in the third-party transcription `omarjazaa/The-Pragmatic-Programmer-Book`, `content/topics/topic-09.json`); 97 Things Every Programmer Should Know, thing_30 "Don't Repeat Yourself" (97-things/97-things-every-programmer-should-know `en/thing_30/README.md`, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0) — "DRY can be applied to structures, such as database schema, resulting in normalization." · reception: not contested. Denormalization for performance is the standing counter-practice. The same 97 Things essay admits it "only where it directly addresses an actual rather than an imagined problem". The card admits a stored copy wherever its source cannot change or a mechanism recalculates it on every change of its inputs, which covers a cache kept for speed when it is an input-keyed memo; a hand-maintained cache, which the formulation admits 'for performance reasons' when 'not exposed to the outside world', is not admitted, since no openable source states it and the UI guidance rejects it. The topic's other proposed formulation locators are not named as the card's formulation: Clean Code ch. 12 "No Duplication" (isEmpty returning 0 == size()), APOSD ch. 2 §2.2 (an emphasis shade specified apart from the colour it derives from) and TAOUP ch. 4 "The SPOT Rule" corollaries (caching as possibly premature optimization). The card follows none of their wording, and TAOUP's caching caveat is carried by the openable 97 Things essay. · notes: confidence moderate. The evidence is official documentation of three kinds. The first is one UI framework's normative guidance, with worked bug examples: the packing-list counter, the selected-item label and the mirrored prop. The second is one database's generated-column mechanism. The third is one language's cache documentation and FAQ. No empirical defect measure for stored derived values is carried. The run's search budget was exhausted, so no paper search was re-run; the topic's candidate papers concern code clones, not derived data. The guidance is written for UI component state. Its extension to objects, records and database rows rests on its own normalization analogy and on the generated-column and cached_property mechanisms, which the card's Source caveat states. The card's second accepted case is limited to a copy that a mechanism recalculates on every change of its inputs (a generated column, useMemo, an lru_cache keyed through `__eq__`/`__hash__`); a copy refreshed by hand in each write path is flagged, as the packing-list solution directs. Severity major rests on the documented bugs and the "less error-prone" statement, not on a measured rate. Two conditions are not carried. One is the "actual, not imagined, problem" condition on denormalization for speed, which is formulation only. The other is the framework's memoization threshold ("If the overall logged time adds up to a significant amount (say, 1ms or more), it might make sense to memoize that calculation."), a render-time measure for one framework; the card's two accepted cases hold whatever the cost. An emptiness flag computed from a size is not named as a case in the card, since no fetched source names it; the triggers still reach `is_empty`. `cached_property` itself "allows writes", so the card's "nothing else writes the copy" is stricter than the mechanism, and the finder treats a direct write to a cached attribute as one more write path. The triggers are wider than the topic spine's. They add any receiver name (Go receivers, field writes on other objects), compound assignment (`+=`), a `selected` name in field assignments (so a selected element copied out of a list, such as `self.selected_item = self.items[index]`, `this.selectedItem = this.items.find(...)` or `m.selected = m.items[i]`, reaches the card), the SQL `numeric`, `integer` and `bigint` column types, `pub(crate)`, `is_empty` in declarations, Go `sync.OnceValue`/`OnceFunc`, `memoize` and `@cache`/`.cache`. Look-arounds keep `account`, `discount`, `encounter`, `country`, `consumer`, `summary` and `assume` from firing. `useState` keeps every component file with local state in reach, which is where the evidence's examples live. Ownership: a duplicated code block, a repeated literal and a decision encoded in several modules belong to other rules of the topic. A value derived from data held in another table, module or service is outside this card.

(the implementation compares consecutive branches only, and asks for the same comments too) · topic: duplication-and-single-source-of-truth (research/software-craft/duplication-and-single-source-of-truth.md) · formulation: 97 Things Every Programmer Should Know, thing 30 "Don't Repeat Yourself" (Steve Smith; 97-things/97-things-every-programmer-should-know `en/thing_30/README.md`, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/97-things/97-things-every-programmer-should-know/master/en/thing_30/README.md, fetched): "Copy-and-paste *if-then* or *switch-case* logic is among the easiest to detect and correct." · reception: not contested · notes: confidence moderate. Five checkers across Java, Python, Go, JavaScript/TypeScript and Rust agree that identical branches are duplicate code or a probable copy-paste error, but no source measures a fault rate, so severity stays minor. The one-statement exemption comes from S1871 alone: its documentation says "single line of code", the sonar-java implementation counts statements, and the sonar-python check SameBranchCheck (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SonarSource/sonar-python/master/python-checks/src/main/java/org/sonar/python/checks/SameBranchCheck.java, `isOnASingleLine`) and the eslint-plugin-sonarjs check (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SonarSource/eslint-plugin-sonarjs/master/src/rules/no-duplicated-branches.ts, `hasRequiredSize`: `tokens[tokens.length - 1].loc.end.line > tokens[0].loc.start.line`) measure the lines a body spans, so the card's statement unit is sonar-java's. Error Prone, clippy and Ruff also flag one-statement duplicates, and the card's Limits record that other reading. The overlap, guard and binding-type conditions come from clippy's match_same_arms implementation. The fix's placement follows the same merge test: the later arm moves back when no arm between them overlaps it, otherwise the earlier arm moves forward. The card applies them to if chains by analogy, because an if chain also tests its conditions in order. The card does not flag branches that share only leading or trailing statements: the one check for that, branches_sharing_code, is nursery and allow by default, so the card names it only as a bound in its Limits. Consecutive identical conditions (clippy ifs_same_cond) are a control-flow defect and not this card's. The Finding output clause that keeps side-effecting conditions evaluated, joined in their original order with the short-circuit or, is the drafter's guard on the fix and has no source fragment; Error Prone's own suggested fix replaces the whole if with the else branch. Ownership: control-flow owns conditionals, and its evidence layer also opened S1871. If control-flow ships an identical-branch card, DSN-27 defers to it through a DEFER_TO entry. The design note's other formulation locators, Refactoring 2nd ed. §3.2 "Duplicated Code" and Clean Code ch. 17 G5, are dropped: they cannot be opened, and the openable essay carries the formulation. Example: java, good half compiled with javac.

Secrets are assumptions about an implementation that client programs are not allowed to make (paraphrased from [5]). In other words, they are things that can change; the interface defines the things that cannot change (without simultaneous changes to both implementation and client). Obviously, it is easier to program and modify a system if its parts make fewer assumptions about each other. On the other hand, the system may not be easier to design—it’s hard to design a good interface. And there is a tension with the desire not to hide power." / "There is another danger in keeping secrets. One way to improve performance is to increase the number of assumptions that one part of a system makes about another; the additional assumptions often allow less work to be done, sometimes a lot less. For instance, if a set of size n is known to be sorted, a membership test takes time log n rather than n. This technique is very important in the design of algorithms and the tuning of small modules. In a large system the ability to improve each part separately is usually more important." The normative rule rests on a tool rule and on official guidelines (PMD DataClass, C++ Core Guidelines C.2 and C.4, Rust API Guidelines, clippy). The study corroborates only at method level and only as a co-occurrence: it covers Java-only projects, it counts read-only feature envy, and it found no change-proneness rise for that smell. The card narrows PMD's whole-class rule to write-back on a type with an invariant. A holder whose fields vary independently, and which outside code only reads or writes while keeping no condition on its members, neither a bound on one nor a relation among several, stays out of the finding, although PMD would flag it. An immutable record-style carrier is skipped even when its constructor validates, copies or normalizes; a carrier whose fields can be reassigned, such as a data class that is not frozen, is judged by its invariant. Three phrases of the drafted statement were dropped or replaced: "where the holder has a single user, move the data to that user" became PMD's unconditioned "in some other cases"; "a transfer object at a boundary" was dropped because no fetched source names it, and such an object is covered by the no-invariant property and by the skip for a default, clamp or normalization a caller applies to a member only for its own use, which rests on C.2's invariant as a condition a constructor establishes for the public member functions to assume and on C-STRUCT-PRIVATE's passive data structures whose public fields clients can mutate arbitrarily; "query methods that serve co-located behaviour stay allowed" was dropped for want of a fetched source and replaced by C.4's helper that needs no direct access to the representation, limited to a helper that calls only the type's own operations and reads no field or accessor to decide a write back into the object, so that the card's own bad half is not skipped. PEP 557 and C++ Core Guidelines C.2 and C.4 were added as fetched evidence; the PEP 557 `frozen` fragment backs the Limits sentence on carriers whose fields can be reassigned. Sjøberg et al., TSE 2013, DOI 10.1109/TSE.2012.89 (**relayed** only through Palomba 2018 §2: "smells do not always constitute a problem, and that often class size impacts maintainability more than the presence of smells") is not carried in the card. Trigger changes: the record-declaration trigger and `@Getter` were dropped, because a record's fields cannot be reassigned and a getter-only holder cannot receive a write-back. The annotation trigger `@(Data|Setter)\b|@dataclass\b` was dropped, because it names Java and Python annotations that the TypeScript bad half cannot show. Trigger 1 matches any read of the same object inside a setter's arguments, with `set` followed by an upper-case letter or an underscore, so `set_balance(acct.balance() - x)` and `SetBalance(acct.Balance() - x)` match while `cache.set(k, cache.get(k) + 1)` does not. Trigger 3 matches a read of any field of the same object on the right-hand side, such as `order.status = order.total > 100 ? ...`. All four triggers compile under Python re, and each matches one line of the bad half; none matches the good half or the negative lines `self.balance -= x`, `this.setBalance(this.getBalance() - x);`, `cache.set(k, cache.get(k) + 1)`, `if (a.x == a.y) {`, `x.a <= x.b`, `const total = order.total + tax;` and `@DataProvider`. The Example's good half compiles under tsc --noEmit --strict (tsc 6.0.2) with `declare const account: Account; declare const amount: number;` in scope and the elided body filled, and the bad half compiles under the same flags with `Account` declared with `getBalance`, `setBalance`, `withdrawnToday`, `dailyLimit` and `limitReached`.

The candidate empirical studies (Zoller and Schmolitzky, 'Measuring inappropriate generosity with access modifiers in Java systems', IWSM-MENSURA 2012; Vidal et al., 'Understanding and addressing exhibitionism in Java empirical research about method accessibility', Empirical Software Engineering, doi 10.1007/s10664-015-9365-9; 'Over-exposed classes in Java: an empirical study', Computer Languages, Systems & Structures, PII S1477842415300531; Khomh et al., Empirical Software Engineering 17, 2012) could be neither opened nor relayed in this run (search budget spent; no GitHub-hosted copy, none in the neverworkintheory bibliography), so no prevalence figure is carried. The override exemption rests on Error Prone's matcher code rather than on documented text, and on PMD's inherited-member clause; the framework clause generalises Error Prone's dependency-injection case to a framework that accepts a narrower level; the serializer clause rests on Go's `encoding/json` alone; the container clause holds where the language bounds members or items by their container (Java per PMD; Rust items neither re-exported nor leaked per unreachable_pub; Python per PEP 8's containing-namespace rule); the Go specification exports field and method names on their own, and the json encoder reaches exported fields of unexported struct types, so the Limits exempt them. The Rust API guidelines' C-STRUCT-PRIVATE (fetched) is not carried: field exposure and accessors that publish the representation are the topic's other rules. Out of scope and not carried: interface depth and width, the operations and contract of a published API, a mutable internal object handed to a caller, global variables, and encapsulation as a security boundary. The Go example's good half builds with `go build` and `go vet` in a scaffold that supplies `Item` and `Store{src fetcher}`. Triggers broadened from the drafted set: Rust `pub` and restricted `pub(...)` items and fields, TypeScript export lists, Go exported struct fields, Python public `def`, `class` and `self.` attributes, and default-public class-member headers with or without a return annotation; the Go patterns merged into one.

For trivial accessors kept to keep the representation changeable: Code Complete ch. 6 and Effective Java Item 16 (formulation), SonarSource S1104's fix, Rust API Guidelines C-STRUCT-PRIVATE, Effective Go 'Getters', .NET 'Field Design', and the Lombok @Data practice (reception). Holub and Y. Bugayenko, who argue against accessors altogether (reception). The card ships because a sourced condition separates the cases: whether a public attribute can later gain behaviour behind the same access syntax (PEP 8; Google Python §2.13.1 and §2.13.2); where it can and the language's design guidelines admit a public instance field, the property-language guides agree that the pass-through pair goes, and where it cannot (S1104, C-STRUCT-PRIVATE, Effective Go, against C.131) the card does not reach · notes: confidence moderate — the rule rests on fetched official documentation and style guides for the two first-class languages with properties (the Google Python and TypeScript guides state it as a directive, PEP 8 as "it is best", the TypeScript Handbook as "very rarely useful" and "fine"), with C.131 for the definition of trivial and the examples of non-trivial semantics; no empirical measure of cost exists among the sources, so severity stays suggestion and the Caveat names a style cost, not a measured clarity or defect cost. The Thesis adds "whose design guidelines admit a public instance field" because the .NET Field Design guideline forbids public instance fields in a language with properties; there the replacement for a trivial property is not a public field, and the card does not carry that language's form; the Limits' statement of the documented guidance carries the same precondition. The Thesis reaches pairs only: the lone pass-through getter that the Google TypeScript guide also discourages ("consider making it readonly") stays a Limits note, since Google Python §2.13.2 counts a read-only property as a legitimate use. A pair forwarding to a collaborator's member is excluded because the Google TypeScript guide's own good example does that. The Limits and Validator exclude a pair that overrides an accessor or property a supertype defines, implements an abstract property of an abstract base class, or is overridden by a subtype's own accessor, because the fix fails to compile or run there: reproduced with tsc 6.0.2 --strict (TS2610 for a field overriding a base get/set pair, TS2611 for a get/set pair overriding a base field) and python3 (TypeError on instantiating a class whose field replaces an abstract property, AttributeError "property 'size' of 'After' object has no setter" when a field replaces a pair over a base's read-only property); the TypeScript 4.0 release notes, the Python Descriptor Guide and the abc documentation state each mechanism. The Validator skips a getter and setter method pair the change does not add or that code outside the change calls, matching the Limits, because replacing methods with a field changes every call site and PEP 8 ties a public attribute to a commitment to avoid backwards incompatible changes (the skeptic reproduced the gap this closes: a pre-existing `o.get_size()` caller raising AttributeError after an added pair was replaced); a property pair keeps its callers' syntax and stays in reach. The fix renames each use of the backing field in the class and in any subtype or other code that reads or writes it, and rewrites each method-pair call in the change, so that it compiles: the skeptic reproduced TS2339 when a subtype's `this.countValue += 1` was left behind, and the fixed form (`count` renamed in Base and Sub) compiles under tsc 6.0.2 --strict. The Example uses typescript, not the java the series assigned: the rule does not reach Java (no properties), so a Java pair would illustrate the Limits' opposite case; both halves compile with tsc --noEmit --strict --target es2022 (callers `c.count = 3` unchanged across the two). The fifth trigger was narrowed from any `get`/`set` call to a declaration at line start (optional access modifier, name, parameter list, optional return type, opening brace), so that the getter calls in every file of a language the rule does not reach do not dispatch the card; Python accessor methods are caught by the `def (get|set)_` trigger and properties by the decorator trigger; of the five triggers, the second and third match the Example's bad half. The card does not carry public fields in languages without properties, fields exposed wider than their callers need, or a data holder whose behaviour lives elsewhere, which the topic owns as separate rules, nor a mutable internal object returned by an accessor (SpotBugs EI_EXPOSE_REP), which belongs to mutable-state-and-immutability.

Trigger gaps: a call to a member annotated internal, test-only or visible-for-testing has no lexical signature at the call site, and an indirect import of a name another module only imported has no trigger; the developer applies both, and the finder sees them only in a hunk that another trigger brings in.

A result declared with a concrete collection class is outside the rule: SonarSource S1319 flags it ("as a return type of a public method"; "an implementation detail your API should not expose") and PMD LooseCoupling's preferred example returns the interface, while the Python typing best practices prefer concrete types for the return values of concrete implementations (Yes: `-> dict[str, int]`; No: `-> MutableMapping[str, int]`) and the Google Go Style Guide returns concrete types by default; no fetched source states a condition that separates them, which is why the api-design-and-use spine holds return-type-concrete-or-interface as pending-no-separating-condition. For other results the Google Go Style Guide ("Accept interfaces, return concrete types"; "Do not rotely encapsulate without reason") stands against Effective Go "Generality" and the Rust API Guidelines C-NEWTYPE-HIDE, and the card separates them by Effective Go's condition (a type that exists only to implement an interface and will never have exported methods beyond it) and C-NEWTYPE-HIDE's (promising less about how a result is constructed or represented); the Google guide's own Caution (extra details that let the user bypass safety checks; a concrete type that makes changing the underlying provider a breaking change) is recorded in the Limits but not flagged, since the guide says only "you may return an interface". Parameter types are not contested: the Google guide's adage and the Python typing best practices both take abstract types as arguments · notes: confidence moderate. All anchors are official documentation or tool rules opened from this environment; no measured study backs the rule, so the card carries no number. The candidate paper Parnas 1972, "On the criteria to be used in decomposing systems into modules" (doi 10.1145/361598.361623), **unfetched**: it states the general criterion (a module hides a design decision likely to change) but no GitHub-hosted copy was found (tpn/pdfs path guesses 404, papers-we-love design list has no entry, WebSearch budget exhausted), so it is not cited and SWEBOK V3 §1.4 carries the principle. Khomh et al. 2012, Zoller and Schmolitzky 2012 (IGAT/IGAM), Vidal et al. (doi 10.1007/s10664-015-9365-9) and the over-exposed-classes study measure member and class visibility and public data, not the types a signature names, so they belong to the topic's visibility and data-holder rules and were not re-searched for this card. Scope against the drafted statement: "a public function that returns its internal container" is not carried, since collection results are outside the rule (see reception); handing a caller the internal mutable object is left to mutable-state-and-immutability, and the formulation's fix of named operations on the internal map (getParameter) is not carried. "A public struct that embeds a helper type" is not carried: as worded and as detected it held in one language only, and the language-agnostic rule (a type inherits, embeds or dereferences to another type only when every public member it gains belongs in its own interface), on the Uber Go Style Guide's "Avoid Embedding Types in Public Structs" and "Embedding in Structs", is drafted in inheritance-versus-composition (delegate-not-inherit-partial-interface); the Limits leave which members a type gains by inheriting, embedding or dereferencing to their own rules. S1319's third case, a public field typed with a collection class, is left to the topic's field-visibility rule. Parameters rest on S1319, PMD, the CPython typing documentation, the Python typing best practices and clippy ptr_arg. impl Trait is kept in Limits with the guideline's own hedges ("probably", "may"). Triggers changed from the drafted set: the Rust pattern is split into a parameter pattern for collection types and a result pattern for adapter chains; the Java and TypeScript patterns also match parameters; the Python pattern matches parameter annotations only (and `__init__`), so `-> dict[...]` results no longer trigger; the Go pattern also matches New… constructors and no longer names map or slice results, though its lower-case-identifier alternative still matches a `map[...]` result and builtin results, which the Validator sets aside; an exported-class-implements pattern (Java and TypeScript) matches the Example's bad half. Residual: read literally, the Python typing best practices' "prefer concrete types ... for concrete implementations" would also favour returning the implementing class from a Python factory; its examples are built-in collections, so the constructor clause rests on Effective Go's own precondition. Ownership, for the orchestrator: the collection-parameter half overlaps the api-design-and-use draft API-09 (a public operation declares each parameter with the most general type that offers the operations it uses), on the same anchors (PMD LooseCoupling, clippy ptr_arg, CPython typing.rst, the Google Go decisions), and the api-design-and-use note claims concrete versus abstract types in signatures and construction; either drop the parameter half here or record a DEFER_TO. The Example's good and bad halves were compiled with tsc 6.0.2 --noEmit --strict under /tmp/craft-research/dsn-07-rev2/ts-good and ts-bad. The card bundles three shapes (collection parameters, adapter-chain results, constructors returning an implementing type) with separate anchors; splitting is left to the orchestrator.

Nilsson): Design by Contract "helps you ensure a valid state by validating incoming data and the object itself on entry and exit of each public method." · reception: not contested as the default; an explicitly marked unchecked sibling path is an accepted opt-out (C-VALIDATE), carried in the Limits as the separating condition · notes: confidence moderate. The anchors are normative: five SEI CERT Java rules (each tagged draft in the repository's front matter; OBJ05-J rated severity High, OBJ01-J Medium), the Rust API guidelines and official book, one SonarSource rule (a Minor code smell), the contract model of a deferred PEP, and the class-invariant definition a peer-reviewed study adopts; no study measures defects caused by a broken class invariant, and the same ECOOP 2017 study finds class invariants rare in practice (Table 5: 3,793 class-invariant constructs over all versions, 100 in the latest versions, in 5 programs, against 786,723 precondition constructs in 160 programs) — a usage count, not carried in the card. Severity major rests on the CERT rules' statements that exposed fields and leaked mutable references let a class's invariants be violated and its state corrupted, and on ERR03-J's documented incorrect results after a failed method left the object modified. The CERT rules are written for Java and motivated by security; the card carries only their invariant statements, which hold for any type with non-public state, and Python marks non-public members by a naming convention, as PEP 316's definition of public shows. The Go zero-value bound rests on Effective Go, which accepts types whose zero value needs an initializing constructor. The card does not carry: the callback problem (an operation that calls out while the invariant is suspended lets the callee observe the inconsistent state), located only in an abstract with no confirmed identifier ("The dependent delegate dilemma", in the same Google Scholar export); loop invariants and the subtype substitutability rule, which are separate rules of the topic; invariants of state shared between threads, reserved to concurrency correctness; checking a precondition and failing fast, owned by defensive-programming; the assertion form of an invariant check and its removal in optimized builds, judged by their own rules. SWEBOK V3 ch. 3 §4.4 (ligurio/swebok-v3 transcription, fetched) states design by contract with preconditions and postconditions only and does not mention class invariants, so it is a formulation locator, not evidence here; the assertion-density studies (Kudrjavets et al. 2006, Casalnuovo et al. 2015, Catolino et al. 2019) measure assertions, not invariants, and are not cited. The ERR03-J case overlaps the error-handling rule that a handler leaves the program in a valid state; this card owns the type's own public operations, that one the handler.

ERR-12 owns a panic, exit or abort on an expected failure; this card owns the assertion forms, including the ones a build strips.

The card narrows the orchestrator's wording, which said every test configuration keeps the assertions on. The criterion asks for "at least some dynamic analysis", so the card asks for at least one run: a run with assertions off follows the rule while any other test, fuzzing or dynamic-analysis run keeps them on, not only a run of the same tests, and the Validator question and the Finding output use the same threshold. The criterion asks for a configuration "which enables many assertions", so the Thesis forbids only a switch that strips or disables assertions throughout the code under test, and the Limits let a run disable them in named packages, classes or dependencies (java(1) -da with a package or class argument; a Cargo per-package profile override). The card also asks for the enabling switch where the runtime disables assertions by default (java(1)), not only for the absence of a disabling switch. The title follows the same narrowing. The Chromium sentence is about DCHECK() and Chromium's Canary channel; the Rationale keeps its tests-and-developer-machines part and words the rest as whatever pre-release builds keep the assertion. The step facet is test only, since the rule is about how runs are configured, not the shape or description of the change. Not carried: Casalnuovo et al. (ICSE 2015) and Catolino et al. (ICSME 2019), both **relayed**. They are about assert density and defects, or test-class assertion density, and say nothing about running tests with assertions enabled. Go and TypeScript have no assert statement of their own, so the Go example shows a harness that launches the code under test. Scope file cannot see a sibling run in another file, such as tox.ini beside a CI workflow, so a false positive there is left to the verifier. Ownership: whether a test states its own checks with an always-enabled assertion library (Error Prone UseCorrectAssertInTests) belongs to test quality, and whether assertions stay on in production is left open.

Closing edits after the second review, applied as worded: the Validator skips an operation the codebase's means cannot mark, such as a method the checker's configured list cannot name, and the Limits put an operation the list cannot name outside the rule, both resting on the `stringmethods` flag text, now quoted in the Source, and on unusedresult.go lines 159-175; the set.add flag is named by the polarity the doc states ("false" when the element was already contained) in the Rationale and as "the flag returned by adding to a set" in the Limits. The Rust policy is the standard library's own and the card carries it to any library; "Most methods are like concat" is carried only as the broad side's position. Go dispatch rests on the `unusedresult` line alone, so a new Go function whose list lives in an untouched configuration file is not dispatched

The evidence is official design guidance from two ecosystems (the Rust API Guidelines; the Google Go Style Guide), official language documentation from three (the TypeScript Handbook, the Python `typing` reference, the Go specification), one tool rule (Error Prone) and the SWEBOK Guide; no controlled experiment or measured defect rate is carried. Rice, Aftandilian, Jaspan, Johnston, Pradel, Arroyo-Paredes, "Detecting argument selection defects", OOPSLA 2017 (DOI 10.1145/3133928) and Pradel and Gross, ISSTA 2011, on equally-typed argument order, are **unfetched** (no GitHub-hosted copy, no relayed snippet, WebSearch budget spent) and are not cited; the relayed API-usability papers in the candidate list (Piccioni, Furia, Meyer, ESEM 2013; Stylos and Myers, FSE 2008; Ellis, Stylos, Myers, ICSE 2007; Myers and Stylos, CACM 59(6) 2016, DOI 10.1145/2896587) state nothing about parameter types and are not carried. Scope as the rule was proposed, with two narrowings: the swap clause covers two or more parameters of one primitive representation that differ in meaning or unit, although C-NEWTYPE's own example is a single `Miles` parameter; and the closed-set clause covers a fixed set of named alternatives (an enumeration or a union of literals), leaving a range-checked wrapper type such as C-VALIDATE's `Ascii` to contracts and defensive programming. C-CUSTOM-TYPE's own example is two boolean arguments; boolean flag parameters stay with routine-size-and-parameters and parameter count with the same topic. The named-argument alternative rests on the Go option-structure guidance alone, which frames it for long signatures and says the techniques "may be unnecessary for your use case"; the card offers it as one way to satisfy the rule, never as a requirement, and names no language mechanism for it (keyword arguments, builders and functional options stay out of the prose). The Thesis states the alternative's effect as the guidance states it, harder to swap: the Go specification, Struct literals, allows a literal without keys whose "element list must contain an element for each struct field in the order in which the fields are declared", so an options value alone does not make every caller name each field. The Limits carry five language traits sourced from official documentation: an alias that the checker treats as identical gives no distinction (TypeScript, Python), a distinct type checked only by a static type checker holds only where that checker runs (Python), a checker that compares types by their members accepts one same-shape wrapper for another unless each declares a private member (TypeScript), a defined type still accepts any representable untyped constant (Go), and an enumeration over numbers is compatible with numbers (TypeScript). The role-only exclusion (width and height) rests on the Error Prone page's own legitimate-swap example. The Example's good half was compiled with `rustc --emit=metadata`, and a swapped call against it fails with E0308, while the bad half compiles. The triggers widen the proposed set: the C-family pair pattern also matches a pair after the first parameter, the Go pattern also matches `a T, b T`, the closed-set pattern is case-insensitive, matches a suffix (`sortMode`) and the Java and Go forms, and the unit pattern matches Java and Go declarations as well.

The evidence is official documentation across five ecosystems (Go, Rust, .NET, Java, TypeScript, plus Kotlin), one analyzer rule and one misuse-detection study's abstract; it states the mechanism and the designs, and none of it measures how often an unenforced call order causes a defect. The detector figures come from the reviewer's summary on the It Will Never Work in Theory page, not from the abstract, and they cover API misuses of every kind, not call-order misuses alone. Compared with the original statement: "an error that names the missing step" became an error that says the object is not in an appropriate state, because the Java and .NET exception guidance says only that; the Kotlin lateinit text backs only the Rationale's "can identify" and the Finding output's fix. The Rust book sentence became the Limits' trade-off sentence, and the book's encapsulated workflow, where a call out of order has no effect, became a Limits case so that the finder does not flag it. Invariants and preconditions are left to the contracts topic, named in the card only as "a precondition … is outside the rule". The relayed API-usability papers (Piccioni et al. ESEM 2013, Stylos and Myers FSE 2008, Ellis et al. ICSE 2007, Myers and Stylos CACM 2016) are not cited because none of their relayed statements is about call order. A controlled study comparing required constructor parameters with create-set-call (Stylos and Clarke, ICSE 2007, from memory, **unfetched**) could not be searched this run. The card's any-order-properties branch keeps create-set-call admissible, so the study would not contradict the rule. Triggers differ from the computed facets: capitalised first letters for exported set-up methods, a declaration-form trigger that catches set-up methods taking parameters (the Example's bad half matches through it), with a second alternative for a method declared without a keyword, as in TypeScript classes, a state-flag trigger that accepts any receiver name, and `(?i)` on the doc-comment and message triggers.

Official guidance from three ecosystems agrees on keeping non-public what only the module itself uses: PEP 8 and the Google TypeScript and Go style guides. PEP 8 also states the uneven cost of narrowing a public name later, and the Rust book states privacy by default as the way to hide implementation details. None of them measures a cost, and no API-usability paper could be confirmed this run because the WebSearch budget was used up. The in-doubt clause is stated for a class's attributes and the Go clauses for interface types; the card reads both for every name a module exposes. No Java source on access modifiers was opened: the dev.java language tutorial is not in the public `java/devjava-content` repository, and docs.oracle.com is denied. The Java reach therefore rests on the shared mechanism. The test clause keeps the Go guide's own terms (back door, test double) and leaves it to the finder to judge what a back door is. It does not exclude test uses in general, because the TypeScript guide's "used outside of the module" admits them. Module depth and interface width belong to their own topic. Narrowing a surface that is already published also belongs to its own topic, and the card's Limits confine the rule to names the change adds or makes public. The trigger set is broad and matches the common declaration heads of exported or public names in the five languages; a Rust or Go struct field, a TypeScript class field without a modifier, a Python module-level variable, a Java interface member and a restricted Rust visibility such as pub(crate) reach the finder only in a hunk another trigger selects. The Validator narrows it to names added to the public surface.

The card reads it for TypeScript overloads and Python typed overload declarations by the same mechanism. A branch for Java interface and abstract methods with no access modifier (ends in a semicolon, has at least one typed parameter, excludes return/throw/new/else/await/yield/assert/case) and a TypeScript call/construct-signature branch are added, because the Validator names a signature that ends in a semicolon with no body; tested against the lines listed above. The evidence is official and style documentation for Go, Java, TypeScript and Rust, the mypy type checker's documentation for Python, and two SpotBugs patterns written for Java; no source measures a defect rate, and the card carries no number. severity major follows the evidence tying in-band values and unchecked nulls to bugs ("can lead to bugs", "a major source of bugs", "will most likely break client code"). The type-alias clause rests on the Google TypeScript guide alone and is stated for a union with a null or undefined type, which reaches TypeScript and Python type hints. The relayed candidate papers (Piccioni, Furia, Meyer, ESEM 2013; Stylos, Myers, FSE 2008; Ellis, Stylos, Myers, ICSE 2007; Myers, Stylos, CACM 59(6) 2016, DOI 10.1145/2896587) are not carried: their relayed statements concern API-usability methods, method placement and factories, not absence in a return type. Triggers: the third pattern (a -1, zero or empty-string default after `=>`, `??`, `unwrap_or(`, `map_or(` or `orElse(`, or after a comma in `getOrDefault(` or `get(`) was added so that an expression-bodied in-band return, as in the Rust example, dispatches the card; the alias pattern also matches `None` and a null that leads the union. The search-comparison trigger leads the finder to the called routine; the card does not flag a caller's misuse of a library string function's sentinel, because the rule judges the operation's declaration. An unannotated Python routine has no declared result type, so the finder flags its unmarked None for a no-result outcome and the fix adds the `| None` annotation. The Rust Example's good half compiles with rustc --emit=metadata inside a struct holding `ports: HashMap<String, i32>`.

The style guide's use of non-const pointers for optional outputs is not carried. Parameter count is left to routine-size-and-parameters and failure reporting to error-and-exception-handling. The evidence is seven fetched official documents: style guides for Go and Python, PEP 8, the .NET property guideline and the CA1024 analyzer rule, the Kotlin conventions and the Rust conversion-naming guideline. They agree, but each is a recommendation ("can be used", "Avoid", "AVOID", "should probably", "Prefer", "preferable"), none measures a cost, and CA1024 is off by default, so the severity is minor. The relayed API-usability papers among the topic's candidates (Piccioni et al., ESEM 2013; Stylos and Myers, FSE 2008; Ellis, Stylos and Myers, ICSE 2007; Myers and Stylos, CACM 2016, DOI 10.1145/2896587) do not state this claim and are not cited. The card does not carry the following. (1) "Blocking input or output" in the orchestrator's wording became "a time-consuming operation perceivably slower than reading a field" (CA1024) together with "complex computation or remote call" (Go), because no fetched fragment names file or database input or output; the Validator lists those as instances. (2) "load" was dropped from the work-naming words, because only compute and fetch are sourced. (3) The Swift remedy of documenting the complexity of a non-O(1) computed property is formulation only, and no admissible source in the five languages makes documentation sufficient. (4) Kotlin's same-result condition is quoted in the Rationale but is not a Thesis clause. CA1024's conversion, side-effect, order, differing-results and array criteria are left out, because state changes belong to the query-naming card and the rest lie outside the rule's statement. (5) The no-failure and no-precondition clauses rest on the .NET property guideline and the Kotlin "Does not throw", both written for properties, and hold for properties and getter accessors only. In a language that has properties, the Kotlin conventions ("Prefer a property over a function when the underlying algorithm: Does not throw. Is cheap to calculate"), CA1024 ("In these situations, a method is preferable to a property"; "The method performs a time-consuming operation") and Google Python Style Guide §3.15 ("they should be used when getting or setting the variable is complex or the cost is significant"; "such as `get_foo()`") place costly or throwing work in a method, including a get-prefixed method with no arguments, so that shape is set aside. In a language without properties, the getter clause rests on the Go Style Guide §Getters alone, at its threshold of a complex computation or a remote call. The indexer exception follows the .NET text. (6) A get-named routine that takes arguments is left out, although the Go guidance covers any function, because the card holds a routine called as a method to the getter clause only where the language has no properties, and there it takes the no-argument shape the Go guidance names (a noun in place of Get). (7) The Validator sets aside a lock held only around a field read. This follows from the trivial-work condition, not from a fragment. (8) The input-output vocabulary trigger runs on any added network, file, database or sleep call by design, to reach a body changed under an unchanged accessor name. The accessor shapes of the five languages share one alternation, which takes any Rust &self method and any Go method with no arguments, because their getters carry no prefix. The good half of the Example compiled under go vet (go1.24.7) in /tmp/craft-research/api-design-and-use/api-accessor-shape-promises-cheap-access/fix/work/ex.

The card narrows the original statement where the evidence did: the original's "its declared type admits null, None, nil or undefined" becomes a declared type that marks the value as possibly absent (an optional or nullable type, a union with null, None or undefined, or a nullable annotation), and a bare reference or pointer type, where every such type admits absence, does not on its own make a value possibly absent, since NullAway assumes every unannotated parameter, return value and field non-null and asks for @Nullable where one may be null, nilness reports only where the control-flow graph shows nil, SA5011 only a pointer also checked against nil elsewhere, and SpotBugs a null that reaches the dereference on a branch or a return value that should generally be checked; the title says a null test elsewhere "says" the value can be absent, since SA5011 says such a test "suggests" it; a dereference before a later null test is carried as SpotBugs' disjunction (the test is redundant or the dereference is erroneous), decided by the declared type and the producing call, not as a defect outright; an operation the language defines on the absent value (ranging over or taking the length of a nil slice or map, indexing a nil map) is set aside from the Go specification; and the original's handling clause "a value the caller can tell apart from a real result" is left out of the Thesis, which no fetched fragment states, and handed to the rules on substitute values. The Rationale keeps the Handbook's subject, "the lack of checking", rather than making it the programmer's omitted test, since the Handbook sentence sits under §"strictNullChecks off" and may mean the language's checking, and keeps NullAway's "a series of type-based, local checks" rather than confining the checks to dereferences, since its example also reports a call site that passes null. "Throws" among the ways an absent branch leaves the path generalizes SA5011's "will not continue execution after a call to panic or log.Fatal". Osman et al., SANER 2016, DOI 10.1109/SANER.2016.57, was not opened (no GitHub-hosted copy, search budget spent) and is not cited. Example: the good half compiles with tsc 6.0.2 `--noEmit --strict --target es2020` beside `interface Item { id: string; owner: string }`; the bad half fails with TS2532 "Object is possibly 'undefined'". Triggers: the four from the topic facets plus `\b\w+\?:\s*[\w\[{(]` for an optional member or parameter; the first matches the bad half; the third's bare-pointer-parameter alternative `\w\s+\*[\w.]+\s*[,)]` now only dispatches the card, since a bare pointer type does not by itself mark a value as possibly absent, and is kept because a pointer parameter is where a nil test or a nil-returning call is likely to follow.

But use `unwrap()` when `expect()` would lead to noise."). The separating condition is sourced from the Rust book ch. 9.3 and the Google TypeScript guide (a guarantee from local logic, with the reason written) and from the opt-in status of every ban (clippy restriction group, the typescript-eslint strict configuration, the golangci-lint default set, the Uber TODO) · notes: confidence moderate. Official documentation in four languages (Rust book and core docs; Google TypeScript guide and TypeScript Handbook; Effective Go and the Go spec; Python typing docs and mypy) and a Java tool rule (SpotBugs BC_UNCONFIRMED_CAST) agree that a forced form is acceptable only where program logic ensures the value. The requirement to state the reason rests on the Rust book, the Rust core docs and the Google TypeScript guide alone: SpotBugs and Effective Go state the guarantee but not the comment, and no fetched Java source asks for a comment at a cast. No source measures how often an unguarded forced form fails. Severity major follows the orchestrator's default and the sources' crash statements (Google TS "can cause your program to crash at runtime", the Go spec's run-time panic, Option::unwrap "may abort the entire program"); SpotBugs files its cast patterns under STYLE and clippy's bans are restriction lints, which a verifier may weigh. Scope is file: the finder reads the enclosing routine, because a check more than three lines above the change lies outside the hunk context, and at hunk scope the Validator flagged a guarded lookup whatever its stated reason. Java coverage: SpotBugs anchors downcasts, and the Optional javadoc documents only that get() and orElseThrow() throw. Triggers: six patterns — postfix `!` followed by a member access, a closing parenthesis, a comma, a semicolon, a closing bracket or brace, an index other than a `vec![` macro, or the end of the line; unwrap/expect including `_err` and `_unchecked`, `orElseThrow()`, and `.get()` on an optional-named receiver or on the result of a find…, max, min or reduce call (such as `repo.findById(id).get()`); the single-value type assertion; `as` to a capitalized or primitive type; `cast(`; and a parenthesized cast to a capitalized type. A bare `.get()` is left out because it would dispatch the card on nearly every Java diff (Future, Supplier, atomics), so an Optional.get() on a receiver neither named as an optional nor returned by such a call is missed. A definite-assignment assertion (`x!: T`) is not matched either. The triggers compile, parse through cardlib, and the type-assertion pattern matches the bad half's assertion line. Checked with Python re on 32 positive and 37 negative lines: the set matches every positive, among them `text.match(/\d{4}/)![0]`, `this.items![0]`, `${name!}`, `repo.findById(id).get()` and `repo.findById(request.getId()).get()`, and skips `vec![1, 2, 3]`, `println!(...)`, `#![allow(dead_code)]`, `![img](a.png)`, `x != y`, `!ok`, `a!==b`, `f"{value!r}"`, `future.get()`, `ref.get()`, `supplier.get()`, `counter.get()`, `x.unwrap_or(0)` and `expect(result).toBe(3)`; the one false hit found is `smallvec![1,2]`. Example: the Go good half passes gofmt -l and go vet (go1.24.7) with exit 0 and returns the error for a non-string; the bad half passes go vet and panics at run time. validate-craft-cards.py reports 0 errors (a numbering-gap warning only, from validating the card alone). Not carried in the card: the Uber guide (a company style guide outside the source policy's official-documentation list) and the Gallant post, both kept to the reception; the academic candidates (Casalnuovo et al., ICSE 2015; Osman et al., SANER 2016, DOI 10.1109/SANER.2016.57; Estler et al., FM 2014, arXiv 1211.4775), since none states a claim about forced unwraps or casts and WebSearch was exhausted. Ownership: a stop on an expected, recoverable failure belongs to the error-handling card on returning recoverable failures (shipped ERR-12); trust-boundary validation to security-hygiene-in-ordinary-code; an unchecked dereference with no forced form written, and assertion statements and their removal in optimized builds, to their own defensive-programming and contracts cards

Ruff's rule belongs to the pytest-style plugin and its examples are test functions, but it is dispatched on every assert statement. Ruff's README says its default set covers "`F`, `E`, `B`, `UP`, and `RUF` ... as well as many more", which does not settle whether PT018 is on by default, so the card claims only its pedantic category. The card reads "joined by and or or" as and in a must-hold condition and or in a fail-when condition: Ruff splits `a and b` and `not (a or b)` but leaves `a or b or c` whole, and Guava's Javadoc shows the if/throw form testing the inverse of the check call. The range exception rests on OpenJDK's checkIndex, which tests both bounds and reports either with one message, and the computed-message exception rests on Guava's badPositionIndexes. The sibling reference "judged by ERR-01" in the rule's original statement is carried as "judged by their own rules" for self-containment. A fifth trigger was added to the four given. It matches a fail-when conditional joined by or whose throw, raise or panic follows on the same line (`if (a < 0 || b < 0) throw ...`), or whose body opens on the next line (`if size == 0 || name.is_empty() {`, `if not name or size <= 0:`), which is the layout gofmt, rustfmt and black give every such check. It also matches a fail-when conditional that negates a conjunction (`if not (a and b):`, `if (!(a && b))`), and it matches 0.545% of the Go standard-library lines outside tests, testdata and vendor and 0.213% of the Python 3.13 standard-library lines. A sixth trigger matches an assertion or precondition call whose arguments open on the next line, the layout rustfmt gives the Example's own bad line and black gives a long assert. The first, third and sixth triggers also name Spring's Assert.isTrue and Assert.state (spring-projects/spring-framework main, spring-core/src/main/java/org/springframework/util/Assert.java, fetched), Apache Commons Lang's Validate.isTrue and Validate.validState (apache/commons-lang master, src/main/java/org/apache/commons/lang3/Validate.java, fetched) and anyhow's ensure!, the error-returning counterpart of assert! (dtolnay/anyhow master, src/macros.rs, fetched). A seventh matches a continuation line that begins or ends with a logical operator, the layout of a wrapped condition (0.070% and 0.220% of those lines). The candidate papers (Casalnuovo et al. on asserts, Osman et al. on null checks, Estler et al. on contracts) do not state this claim and were not used.

Google Testing on the Toilet, "Exercise Service Call Contracts in Tests" (2018), unfetched and named from memory as repeating the preference for the owner's fake or the real implementation over hand-written stubs; "Increase Test Fidelity By Avoiding Mocks" (2024), relayed (https://testing.googleblog.com/2024/02/increase-test-fidelity-by-avoiding-mocks.html): "The main recommendation is to increase test fidelity by avoiding mocks and using the real implementation or a fake instead." · notes: confidence moderate. The anchors are two tool rules, a mocking library's own annotation contract, a style guide and the client owner's documentation that contests it, all fetched except the AWS v2 guide, which is relayed. No measured study backs the rule: a search for Spadini et al. (MSR 2017) relayed only its abstract, which states no preference, so the card carries no number and no frequency claim. Scope was narrowed on review. The preference for the owner's testing library and the real client is kept only for a component reached through a client over a transport, which is the scope the style guide gives. The general preference for an owner's or the repository's fake over a mock, for any dependency, is not carried; it is recorded as a pending entry with SEG ch. 13 "Faking" as its formulation. The narrowing also leaves out mocks of first-party wrappers, which the Mockito wiki "How to write good tests" (fetched, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wiki/mockito/mockito/How-to-write-good-tests.md) recommends in place of mocking "a type you don't own"; the card's Limits state that bound. A second review found the transport condition contested by the client's owner: the AWS SDK for Go documents stubbing its service client through an interface it publishes (v1 `s3iface`) or one callers define (v2 guide), so the Limits exempt a stub built the way the client's owner documents and keep the condition for a client whose owner documents no such pattern. grpc-go's own Documentation/gomock-example.md (fetched at tag v1.30.0, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/grpc/grpc-go/v1.30.0/Documentation/gomock-example.md: "Idea: Mock the client stub that connects to the server."; 404 at v1.40.0) once documented the same pattern for generated RPC clients; it was removed, so it is not cited in the card. SEG ch. 13 "When Is Stubbing Appropriate?" also calls stubbing a credit-card-server client appropriate; it is a formulation source and stays out of the card. The all-methods condition carries S5969's bound of more than one non-private method, counted on one instance, so the Example's one-method `Doer` is flagged under the transport condition only; net/http's owner documents no interface for stubbing its client (src/net/http/client.go, fetched, has no such pattern) and ships net/http/httptest. S5969 is a Java rule on mocking-framework mocks, both do-not-mock markers are Java annotations and the style guide is written for Go; the card carries each to other languages, as the Source caveat states. The formulation's "those duplicates tend to break the API's contract" is carried only as the mechanism the style guide states ("the complexity of imitating client behavior correctly"), without the "tend to". The Example's good half (an httptest server with the real client, net/http's own testing library) was checked with gofmt, go vet and go test under /tmp/craft-research/tst-02-draft3/goex. The bad half's stubbed `&http.Response{StatusCode: 200}` has a nil Body, which the `http.Client.Do` contract ("the Response will contain a non-nil Body") excludes, so a Fetch that closes the body panics on it. The title says "type" rather than "class" so it holds in languages without classes. The card bundles three conditions with separate evidence; splitting it into three cards is left to the orchestrator.

The card narrows the relayed formulation's "fixed types, such as those defined by the runtime or external libraries" to third-party packages and leaves the language's standard library out of reach, because the fetched anchors speak of third-party libraries and doubles of clocks, files and standard collections fall to this topic's in-process-collaborator and value-object rules. The card states the broader principle (verify only calls made for their side effects) in the Thesis's first sentence as guidance for the developer, but the Validator does not flag it, because deciding whether an unstubbed call is a query and whether its effect is observable needs semantic tracing. The Rationale states the redundancy only for an outcome the code under test reaches only with the stubbed value: when a path that skips the call yields the same outcome, the outcome assertion passes on the skip and the verification is the only check, so the fix asks for a stubbed value no skipping path yields. The Rationale states the study's population as one language and one mocking framework (§ 3.1 admits only Java projects that declare Mockito). The Limits carry the cases where the documented argument does not hold: count and order checks; a call made for its side effect whose returned value only reports whether the effect succeeded and which the code under test checks, where the stub keeps the code under test on its success path, a skipping path can end in the same outcome and the verification is the only check of the effect (the study's § 6.1 observes side-effect calls whose return value is checked only to confirm success; the SEG formulation draws the line at state-changing functions); specific-argument checks on an any-argument stub; and whole-double strictness checks. The Rationale lays the redundancy on the verification only where an asserted outcome needs the stubbed value, and on the stub where the code under test does not use the value (the second branch of the Mockito argument: "it should not be stubbed"). Scope: the defect is live in dynamically typed mock libraries and in statically typed code where a cast via an unchecked type or an untyped module factory bypasses the compiler; a double created from the class or interface in a statically typed language already meets the rule. The card does not carry behavioural fidelity of a double (a double that returns what the real type never returns) — speccing checks shape only and no fetched source states a checkable behaviour rule; nor the @DoNotMock theme of type owners forbidding doubles, which belongs to mocking what you own. The "misspelled assertion helper" claim is hedged in the card because the Python library has raised on a fixed list of assert-prefix misspellings since 3.5 (documented under the `unsafe` parameter); the claim still holds for other misspellings and other libraries. The cast clause rests on no-unsafe-type-assertion, whose own When-Not-To-Use-It admits heavy reporting in stub-heavy test files; a team that accepts that trade uses the project-tolerance Limit. A direct cast to the real type is not in the rule: tsc 6.0.2 (strict) still compares the literal with the type, and the example's jest.fn() literal cast directly to the type fails with TS2352 after a member rename, though a subset literal whose members are plain functions of the member types still compiles under a direct cast (a jest.fn() subset literal fails with TS2352 even before any rename); the card targets the cast through an unchecked type (`as unknown as`, `as any`), which switches the comparison off entirely. The compile-time forms fail only where the test files are type-checked; the Jest "Via babel" passage is the source for that Limit. flake8-mock-spec TMS020–TMS022 and the S9137 implementation (sonar-python python-checks/src/main/java/org/sonar/python/checks/tests/MocksShouldUseAutospecCheck.java, hasReplacement) treat a patch with an explicit new or new_callable as compliant; with an explicit replacement, patch ignores spec and rejects autospec. Triggers 1, 2 and 5 are the Python and Ruby spellings and cannot match the TypeScript Example; each was checked against a bad line of its own language (S9137's `payments = Mock()` and `with patch("app.notify.send") as send:`, flake8-mock-spec's `mocked_foo = mock.Mock()`, an RSpec `double("book")`) and matches none of the compliant forms (`create_autospec(...)`, `patch(..., autospec=True)`, `Mock(spec=...)`, `MagicMock(spec_set=...)`, `instance_double(...)`).

(fetched) · topic: test-doubles (research/software-craft/test-doubles.md) · formulation: Mock Roles, not Objects — "Only mock your immediate neighbours" and "Too many mocks" (fetched) · reception: not contested · notes: confidence moderate; the partial-double half rests on a mocking framework's official guidance plus a four-system practice observation and one framework developer's view, from a study that counted mocks and not spies, none measuring a defect rate or a cost; the chain half rests on the same guidance, which says a chain "hints at" a Law of Demeter violation or a mocked value object, and on an experience report — the card keeps it a hint and bounds it in Limits (an object the unit obtains by design from a factory, pool or connection is created through its neighbour, not navigated to; a returned double that is only verified is outside the chain); the Limits bound on created objects rests on §4.9 of the same paper; its §1.2 excludes returned references from an object's immediate neighbours, so the card does not call a created object an immediate collaborator; the third-party-interface exception is carried for partial doubles only: the RETURNS_DEEP_STUBS javadoc names legacy code alone, and §4.1 of the OOPSLA paper says not to mock types defined by external libraries. The card does not carry the "Too many mocks" count check because no source gives a threshold. The Python `unittest.mock` examples (cpython `Doc/library/unittest.mock-examples.rst`, "Mocking chained calls", fetched from https://raw.githubusercontent.com/python/cpython/main/Doc/library/unittest.mock-examples.rst) document chained-call mocking as a capability and add "Of course another alternative is writing your code in a more testable way in the first place..."; not read as contesting. Go has no built-in partial mocking, so the Go Example shows the chain half only; the good half was compiled with `go vet` and run with `go test` against the `go.uber.org/mock/gomock` package in a scope that declares `User`, `Account` and a generated-style `MockStore`. The card does not carry the §4.7 heading as a general limit on which dependencies a test may double: §4.7 limits expectations on the objects a unit navigates to, §5.1 separates mocks from stubs, and a test that runs a real collaborator and doubles a dependency behind it is left unjudged.
